en: (Keming) Humbly taking this as my guiding principle, I have composed this letter to present to you, Great Layman. I look up to your great teaching for the benefit of sentient beings;
I believe that only the wisdom of Prajñā-emptiness can guide the myriad practices, bring blessings to all living beings, and dispel the burdens of delusion.

Reaching the ultimate principle across the four locations and sixteen assemblies, this Way is fully manifested; from the crushing of the myriad existences to the sweeping away of all into non-being, the Vajra-power is the most firm and sharp.
Therefore, people of the world frequently maintain its recitation. Its responses in both the hidden and the manifest are too numerous to be easily enumerated.
There are six scriptures for translation and three treatises for exposition; according to the capacities of beings, their perspectives differ, and thus variations and similarities persist.
Our Great Master Tiantai, whose wondrous realization penetrated the scriptures, composed this commentary to explain the Qin version; during the chaos and separation of the Five Dynasties,
it flowed eastward to the sea, where various masters produced their own accounts, all of which relied upon various treatises to patch together the divergent translations.

This commentary was fragmented and could not be fully transmitted; subsequently, some even regarded it as spurious, though Zhua’an once strenuously defended it and people only then began to believe and accept it.
Recently, while I was reading this commentary at the Guanshi (Observation Hall) in Nanhu, I was filled with irrepressible joy and remarked:
"The 'Distinction' is truly the *upāya* (expedient means), while the two cycles clarify the ten matters of the inconceivable; these constitute the sequential sections."

I judge that none but the Great Master could have achieved such a work; looking back at the compositions of other schools, although they all share the noble intention of propagating the teachings, none can equal it.
There was a monk named Shanyi who courageously sought out donations, subsequently searching for alternative copies to collate with this edition, which was then carved into woodblocks for publication.
After remaining at Nanhu, Dugu formerly established lecture sessions there; however, due to a fire in the city, the wooden printing blocks were consumed by flames, which was deeply lamented.

Now, having received your instructions, I learn that you have been diligently engaged in investigation and intend to draft a preface for the scriptures so they may be easily consulted—truly an extraordinary undertaking.
As I am about to publish them, I have received your communication and am thus able to examine their general outline.
I have thus offered this commentary, desiring that it be transmitted far and wide for the benefit of the fourfold assembly; this cannot be achieved abruptly.
I have respectfully transcribed it on a separate sheet and present it to you, earnestly praying that you will examine it in detail. Sincerely yours, (Keming).
Respectfully submitted, (Xingshan). For the sake of convenience in consultation, I have incorporated this preface into the scripture.
When the lecturer Xishan Xushì requested certification (*inka*), he was granted an examination and an exposition of the origins and transmission of this commentary.
Furthermore, on a separate sheet of paper, [the Master] provided annotations to supplement missing phrases and clarify the intended meaning, thereby making it complete.
(Xingshan) Thus, fearing that its source would be obscured, he has published this book together with these notes to encourage the faithful to circulate it.
Jin'gang jing ke shi (An Exegesis on the Sections of the Diamond Sutra), compiled by Xu Xingshan of Siming, respectfully recorded in the year Jiawu of the Zhizhen era.

The Tiantai Master Zhiyi’s brief commentary on the title of the sutra explains that the name *Prajñā* is profound, mysterious, subtle, and difficult to fathom; thus, these metaphors are employed to reveal this deep Dharma.
Regarding the term "Gold" (*jīn*), there are three meanings: first, it is the true among the treasures, supreme and indestructible; second, it is useful for practical application.

Sovereignly crushing and destroying all things, it is pure within and without, appearing with distinct clarity. "Firm" (*kāṭhinya*) signifies the meaning of solidity; this refers to body, life, and wealth. "Body" is the *dharmakāya*;
"life" is the *prajñājīvitendriya* (wisdom-life); "wealth" is the *dharmadhana* (Dharma-wealth). These serve as the functional aids to the path, analogous to the three types of *prajñā*:

the *prajñā of ultimate reality* (*lakṣaṇa-prajñā*), which is the eternally abiding nature of reality; the *prajñā of contemplative observation* (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*), which destroys the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*).
The liberation through the wisdom of letters that deludes is sovereign; these three dharmas are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither identical nor distinct, forming the Secret Treasury.
The Buddha’s three bodies are likewise so: the true mark (*dharmatā*) is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), as in the "Chapter on the Vajra Body" of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra;
the contemplative illumination is the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), as in the passage concerning the Vajra Samādhi that shatters all afflictions.
The "Title" refers to the Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which benefits sentient beings according to their capacities by universally manifesting boundlessly.

What was formerly called "Vajra" refers to the stage where the causal conditions are perfected after the mind of the tenth bhūmi; now it is said that from the initial mind to the final stage, there are six kinds of vajras.
The "Essence" is that if one sees that all marks are non-marks, one sees the Tathāgata; this is the true essence of this sutra. The "Principle" (or "Thesis") is...
The practice of non-characteristic *dāna* based on the wisdom of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is like a person with eyes who, when the sunlight shines brightly, perceives various forms;
this is the cause. That one sees all characteristics as non-characteristics is the fruit. This cause and fruit are both based upon the true mark.

Regarding "function": the function is the breaking of attachments; all forms of clinging are collectively termed "attachment," and by breaking through these delusions regarding characteristics, [the true nature] is revealed.

The "function" (*kāritra*) is likewise inherently unimpeded; this is precisely its "powerful operation" (*balopayoga*). Regarding the characteristics of the teachings (*śāstravyavasthāna*), there are five:

(1) *Mahā*, (2) *Vajra*, (3) *Devaputra-paripṛcchā*, (4) *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, and (5) *Rājanarasiṃha*. Although they differ in their breadth and brevity, they are all equally named *Prajñāpāramitā*.

The term *Mahā* refers to the extensive [version], which traverses everything from form and mind up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), all of which are the Mahāyāna. This present text is a brief exposition of the *Vajra*.

This serves as an analogy. Next, the title *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* is explained in detail: it refers to that which destroys all phenomena within the emptiness of their nature and sweeps away all traces of "one" within ultimate reality.
Being exceedingly firm and sharp, it is called "Vajra" (Diamond); being the wisdom of decisive severance, it is called "Prajñā" (Wisdom).

It signifies knowing that although the myriad forms are manifold, there is no mark of "thing" or "self"; conditioned existence is thus severed, its mechanism stilled, and its illumination rests upon the provisional.
It is named *prajñā*; in the Western [language] it is called *vajra*, also *cakraka*. This is translated as "diamond" (*jin-gang*).
It is said to be sharp iron, and is also called the "instrument of breaking. A Great Sūtra states: "The Buddha told Kāśyapa: 'Your current decisive severing is like a hard blade. It also says:
"When the kalpa-fire arises, all things are consumed; that which remains at the bottom, being sharp and keen, is called the diamond-limit (*vajrānta*)."
Furthermore, it is said that the relics of the Buddhas of antiquity transformed into vajra-maṇis; thus, "hardness" and "sharpness" are taken here as metaphors in general.

The old interpretation states: "The essence is hard and the function is sharp. The hardness of the essence means that the various delusions cannot invade it; the sharpness of the function means that it can destroy all things. Now I ask:
if the essence were only hard and not sharp, and the function were only sharp and not hard, would it then be the case that the essence lacks function and the function lacks essence?
This lack of solidity is indeed neither solid nor sharp. What is meant by "solid and sharp"? The *Śata-śāstra* states: "The eye does not know; the mind does not see.
Since they are individually neither seeing, how can they see when combined? Now, relying on the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, this question is resolved such that there is no obstruction to its meaning.

What is here called "solid and sharp" refers to that which is actually neither solid nor sharp; it is a figurative expression of solidity and sharpness, just as "suffering" is used to refer to that which is not suffering.

Taking impermanence as having permanence as its meaning, and taking emptiness as having non-emptiness as its meaning—this is one such example of spontaneous discourse that need not fear such objections.
Prajñā is like a great mass of fire; it cannot be touched from any side. How, then, can it be definitively established as having essence and function?

Essence and function are neither identical nor different due to their causal conditions: if the essence is firm, the function is also firm; if the function is sharp, the essence is also sharp. Since this is so...
Regarding the clarification of the meaning of non-identical provisional designations (*prajñapti*): if one speaks of the substance as "hard," one is simultaneously speaking of its function as "sharp.

This is one aspect of the meaning of provisional designation. Apart from function there is no substance; apart from substance there is no function. Function is itself quiescence, and quiescence is itself function; there is nothing else that is the substance of functionless function.
Substance presides over function, yet there is also nothing else that is the function of substanceless substance. Function presides over [substance].
Regarding their essence, they are neither identical nor different; because they possess causes and conditions, they may be described as identical or described as different.

To refute the notion of identity, difference is taught; to refute the notion of difference, identity is taught. Identity and difference are spoken of only as provisional designations, intended to lead sentient beings to realize that which is neither identical nor different.

This very state of being neither identical nor different is called the departure from the conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of annihilationism and eternalism; thus, these conceptual proliferations cannot be found.
"Entering" is its solidity, which is able to shatter both eternalism and nihilism; this is its sharpness. Question: What is this *prajñā* that is so solid and sharp? Answer:

On one hand, the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) is *prajñā*; on the other, the emptiness of non-interruption, non-eternality, non-identity, and non-difference—ultimate emptiness—is *prajñā*.
When the myriad marks are all one and entirely exhausted in purity, it is as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "As for *prajñā*..."
The contemplation of the three kinds of true reality consists of contemplating the true reality of words, which is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of the objective realm;
and contemplating that very reality, which is the wisdom of the practitioner. When wisdom reflects upon this true reality, both the wisdom itself and its object are called *prajñā*.
Since words can also serve as the means of expression for this [wisdom], they too are *prajñā*; therefore, it is said that there is no liberation apart from words.

Question: Regarding the three names for the single essence within the same Secret Treasury, why are some translated while others are not? Answer: They are translated as "wisdom" (*jñāna*). Question: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that wisdom (*jñāna*) is light and superficial, whereas *prajñā* is profound and weighty; how can these two be mutually translated? Explanation: The seventy-fascicle *Śāstra* explains Subhūti’s five praises—being "incomparable," "immeasurable," "unequaled," "boundless," and "like space. It clarifies that because the nature of phenomena is empty, it is called "incomparable"; because its characteristics are non-existent, it is called "immeasurable"; because there is no duality, it is called "unequaled"; because it transcends all limits, it is called "boundless"; and because it is free from all conceptualization, it is called "like space. Since these meanings are identical, they are mutually translated as "wisdom. Furthermore, because it is the wisdom that realizes the emptiness of all phenomena, it is called *prajñā*. Because it is the wisdom that realizes the equality of all phenomena, it is called "equality-wisdom" (*samatā-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-duality of all phenomena, it is called "non-dual wisdom" (*advaya-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-arising of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-arising" (*anutpāda-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-extinction of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-extinction" (*anirodha-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-differentiation of all phenomena, it is called "undifferentiated wisdom" (*asambhinna-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-obstruction of all phenomena, it is called "unobstructed wisdom" (*apratihata-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-attainment of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-attainment" (*anupalabdhi-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-manifestation of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-manifestation" (*anabhivyakti-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-discrimination of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-discrimination" (*avikalpa-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-grasping of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-grasping" (*anupādāna-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-abiding of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-abiding" (*apratiṣṭhita-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-dwelling of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-dwelling" (*anālaya-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-existence of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-existence" (*abhāva-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-self of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-self" (*anātma-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-personality of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-personality" (*apudgala-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-living-being of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-living-being" (*ajīva-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-nurturer of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-nurturer" (*apoṣaka-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-doer of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-doer" (*akāraka-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-feeler of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-feeler" (*avedaka-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-knower of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-knower" (*ajānaka-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-seer of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-seer" (*apaśyaka-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-hearer of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-hearer" (*aśrotṛ-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-smeller of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-smeller" (*aghrātṛ-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-taster of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-taster" (*asvādayitṛ-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-feeler of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-feeler" (*aspṛśitṛ-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-conceiver of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-conceiver" (*asaṃjñātṛ-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-thinker of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-thinker" (*amanasikāra-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-mind of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-mind" (*acitta-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-consciousness of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-consciousness" (*avijñāna-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-mental-object of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-mental-object" (*aviṣaya-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-sphere of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-sphere" (*agocara-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-basis of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-basis" (*anāśraya-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-support of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-support" (*anālamba-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-reliance of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-reliance" (*anāśrita-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-clinging of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-clinging" (*aparigraha-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-attachment of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-attachment" (*asanga-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-obscuration of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-obscuration" (*anāvaraṇa-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-defilement of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-defilement" (*asaṃkleśa-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-purity of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-purity" (*avyavadāna-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-arising and non-ceasing of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-arising and non-ceasing" (*anutpādānirodha-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-beginning and non-end of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-beginning and non-end" (*anādyantika-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-duration and non-change of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-duration and non-change" (*asthitivikāra-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-coming and non-going of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-coming and non-going" (*anāgamānirgama-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-birth and non-death of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-birth and non-death" (*ajātimaraṇa-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-existence of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-existence" (*abhāva-jñāna*). Because it is the wisdom that realizes the non-personality of all phenomena, it is called "wisdom of non-personality" (*apudgala-jñāna*). Regarding the explanation of the phrase "incomparable" (*anupama*): it is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*) because it is a measurement; this refers to the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), for it is not wisdom that can measure it.
Therefore, it is called "wisdom. Prajñā is the true reality (*dharmatā*). This explains why it is immeasurable. What is the intent behind its being immeasurable?
It is to clarify that the Prajñā attained by the Buddha is a luminous mirror of true reality, profoundly deep, reaching the furthest limits and the very bottom.
The wisdom of a bodhisattva on the causal stage cannot measure the *prajñā* of the Buddha’s fruition stage;
because this causal wisdom is slight and inferior, it cannot measure the *prajñā* of the fruition stage—how then can you falsely cite the absence of a translation [for *jñāna*] as proof?
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "Wisdom is of three kinds: *prajñā*, *vipaśyanā*, and *jñāna*. These belong to the same category and are distinguished according to their names."
In terms of persons: *prajñā* (wisdom) belongs to sentient beings, while *vipaśyanā* (insight) belongs to all noble ones (*ārya*) and the *jñāna* (gnosis) of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

In terms of phenomena: *vipaśyanā* is general characteristic *prajñā*, while *jñāna* is specific characteristic [wisdom]. *Vipaśyanā* that overturns and destroys characteristics is the translation for "correct knowledge and vision" (*samyag-jñāna-darśana*).
This is precisely the knowledge and vision of general characteristics; when it is distinguished from and emerges as discernment (*prajñā*), it belongs to *prajñā*.

Because sentient beings possess the category of wisdom (*jñāna*), and because the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten stages possess the sense of decisive judgment, they are collectively designated as a single stage.
Furthermore, *pāramitā* is also called *arapamitā*, *pāragā*, and so forth;

it is translated as "crossing to the other shore," "reaching the other shore," or "infinite crossing. This is a provisional name; there is no actual crossing, yet it is called "crossing" because the Buddha has already crossed.
The perfection of wisdom is called "all-knowledge. When a bodhisattva has not yet crossed over, it is not called "crossing";

at the very moment of crossing, it is also not called "crossing," because one does not depart from that which has already been crossed and that which has not yet been crossed. Yet, when it is now said that one has "crossed," this is merely a conventional designation for "crossing.

There are three types of crossing: first, the crossing of practice; second, the crossing of time; and third, the crossing of the fruit. The six perfections, when well-cultivated and brought to fulfillment, constitute the crossing of practice; their completion after three *asaṃkhyeya*-kalpas constitutes the crossing of time.
Taking the time-period as the shore of this world, the attainment of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) is the fruit;
taking birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) as this shore and nirvāṇa as the other shore, with afflictions as the middle current, the Eightfold Noble Path is the boat and raft.

Furthermore, taking stinginess and greed as this shore and the fruit of Buddhahood as the other shore, with generosity (*dāna*) as the river itself and right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*) as the boat and raft. Moreover, taking the grasping of signs (*nimitta*) as this shore...
Signlessness is the far shore, wisdom is the river, and diligence is the boat and raft. To begin with, it is thus;

furthermore, since both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are neither this nor that—because they are neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa—it is said that being far removed from both this and that shore is what is called a *pāramitā*.
Moreover, the Middle Way, which is the double negation of the aforementioned saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, constitutes the two [shores].
The Middle Way between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa is non-duality; both duality and non-duality are this "non-two," and both being neither two nor non-two are that.
Therefore, it is called a *pāramitā-sūtra* because it is far removed from the two extremes as well as the middle way. *Sūtra* is translated as "契經" (*qìjīng*).
The character "經" (*jīng*) is explained as "法" (*dharma*, the teaching) and "常" (*nitya*, the eternal), for it is the heart and mouth of the Sages. Next, regarding the "fascicle" (*biànzhóu*):
The first part consists of one hundred thousand verses; the second part consists of twenty thousand verses and did not come to this land;

the third part consists of eighteen thousand verses, which is the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* (Great Chapter) and is also called the *Prabhāsa* (Emitting Light); the fourth part consists of eight thousand verses, which is the *Svalpikā* (Small Chapter) and is also called the *Mārga-gati* (Course of Practice);
the fifth part consists of four thousand verses, which is the *Ratnolkā-praspharaṇa* (Radiant Praise); the sixth part consists of two thousand five hundred [verses].
The seventh section, consisting of one hundred verses, is the *Devaputraparipṛcchā*; the eighth section, consisting of six hundred verses, is the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā*;
and this [present work], the *Vajracchedikā*, consists of three hundred verses. Master Rui states that these are all teachings of the Tathāgata given according to the capacities of sentient beings.
Since Prajñā transcends all measurement and exceeds all numerical quantities, how could it be described in terms of "one," "many," "four," or "five"? ○
Next, regarding the distinction between "before" and "after," Master Zhaolun’s commentary on the phrase "the *Vajra* before and after" states: "There are five kinds of Prajñā.

This refers to the fact that the initial text speaks of one thousand two hundred and fifty people, whereas the later *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin) speaks of a great number of five thousand people;

because those who receive transformation have increased, the *Mahā* is placed later. If the *Vajra* were placed later, the *Ratnaketuparivarta Sūtra* (Renwang jing) would state: 'First, the *Maha*...'"

The *Haga* (Hua) and the *Vajra* (Jingang) [Sūtras] further provide protective mindfulness and entrustment; as for attaining the eye of wisdom, it seems appropriate that this sūtra be placed later, as there is evidence for both views.
Since the teaching is established according to the capacity of the listener, its breadth or brevity differs.

From the night of his attainment of the Way until the eve of his parinirvāṇa, he constantly preached the *Prajñāpāramitā*, clarifying the principle with equal consistency. If one follows the *Guangzan* (Prasphuta-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra)...

He came [to China] at nineteen, left the household life at thirty, and attained enlightenment at forty-two. On the fifteenth day of the second month, after his meal, he preached the *Prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of the bodhisattvas.
Subsequently, the Dharma Master Kumārajīva translated it during the third year of Hongshi of the Qin dynasty (the eleventh year of the reign of Emperor An of the Jin).
Furthermore, at the end of the Northern Wei, Bodhiruci translated the original text of the treatise in eight fascicles.
The Ten Verses were composed by Maitreya; Vasubandhu provided the prose commentary (*bhāṣya*). In total, there are three fascicles, divided into twelve sections:

1. The Introductory Section; 2. The Section on Being Protected by Mindfulness; 3. The Section on Abiding; 4. The Section on Practice; 5. The Section on the Dharma-body and Non-differentiation; 6. The Section on the Faithful; 7.
The Section on Comparative Measurement and Manifesting Superiority; 8. The Section on Manifesting the Nature; 9. The Section on Benefits; 10. The Section on Severing Doubts.

It is divided into eleven sections for the "Path Without Abiding" (Anupasthita-mārga) and twelve sections for the "Circulation" (Prasaraṇa). These distinctions in the timing of the exposition are merely one method of opening the chapters;
according to this single sūtra, it is opened into three parts: the Introduction (Nidāna), the Main Body (Maula), and the Circulation (Prasaraṇa).

The introduction serves as the *nidāna* (causal origin). Prior to the preaching of the doctrine, there must necessarily be a gradual unfolding through events such as alms-gathering, the emission of light, the raining of flowers, and the offering of canopies.

Since the true teaching has thus been initiated gradually, it is appropriate to present the conditions that gave rise to the teaching; for these are like shadows following forms or echoes responding to sounds. Therefore, there is the formal exposition (*samyag-deśanā*).
Furthermore, this is not intended merely to benefit those of the immediate moment, but is meant to be transmitted far into the future; therefore, there is the [concluding] section.

The circulation [of the text] consists of three sections, each with two introductory parts—both general and specific—the main exposition consisting of two successive cycles, and the circulation through the entrustment and the formal conclusion.
Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of...
The Buddha was accompanied by a multitude of one thousand two hundred and fifty people.

Regarding the fifth point, "Thus have I heard": when the Buddha was about to enter Parinirvāṇa, his attendant questioned him, and the Buddha replied that the phrase "Thus have I heard" should be placed at the beginning of all sūtras;
this was heard directly from the golden mouth [of the Buddha], and thus the matter is not erroneous.

"Also, 'at one time' means that the words accord with principle, and principle is likewise like the words. When principle accords with the occasion and causes people to attain awakening, the Sage does not speak in vain;
his words necessarily meet the capacity of the listener, and for this reason it is called 'one time. 'Buddha' is the name of the Great Master. 'Buddha' has the meaning of 'awakening':
he awakens himself, which differs from ordinary people; he awakens others, which differs from those of the Two Vehicles; [he awakens to] Bodhi..."
Because he has awakened to all things, his enlightenment is fulfilled. Residing in Śrāvastī, the Dharma King moves through the world, traveling in accordance with the needs of sentient beings.
He dwells in the city of Śrāvastī in the kingdom of Kośala. "Śrāvastī" means "Renowned for Objects," as excellent goods abound within this realm and its noble fame resounds far across all lands;
thus it is called "Renowned for Objects. Furthermore, regarding Śāvatthī: in the past, there were two rishis who were brothers, the younger of whom was named...
Śrāvastī is translated here as "Younger Brother"; Abhaya means "Invincible. The city is named after these two individuals.
Regarding the Jeta Grove Anāthapiṇḍada Park: Sudatta purchased the grove and Jeta offered the trees, together establishing the vihāra.
This is extensively recorded in other sūtras. As for the Great Bhikṣus: their holy transformation was not kept secret; those who heard them were bound to have their peers.
Since all have heard [the teaching], it can be clearly understood as being like a forest; there must be the fourfold assembly, though they are not recorded here in brief.

Regarding the "one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus who terrify Māra, beg for alms, and destroy evil": this refers to the three Kāśyapas (one thousand) and Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra (two hundred and fifty).
This is called the "General Preface," intended to provide authentication and inspire faith.
At that time, when it was mealtime, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.

Having completed his sequential begging within the city, he returned to his original location. After finishing his meal, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, arranged his seat, and sat down.

Now, to distinguish the introductory section: it is called "World-Honored One" (*Bhagavān*) because he has fully realized the ten titles mentioned above. Regarding "at the time of eating": this refers to the time when the meal is cooked;
at that time, people in their homes all possess a mind of giving, making it easy for [the Buddha] to generate [compassion]. He puts on the *saṃghāṭī* robe.

The Buddha views the fields as fertile soil with well-defined boundaries and furrows, and thus commands those who have left the household life to wear these garments. Holding his alms bowl, he is accompanied by the Four Heavenly Kings.
Regarding the method of entering the city of Śrāvastī with the alms-bowl one carries to beg for food: although the Dharma-body has no need for anything, why must it beg for food?
The sublime offerings of devas and humans, consisting of a hundred flavors, fill [the bowl] daily; yet, one personally practices *piṇḍapāta* (alms-gathering) as is appropriate for meritorious things.

There are ten benefits to begging for food: first, beholding the marks and signs of physical excellence; second, removing illness; third, eliminating pride; fourth, acting as a guardian for women; fifth... [and so forth].
The dragon [dwells] within the alms bowl of the sixth of the Four Heavenly Kings. Seventh, it is equal toward the wealthy and the poor; eighth, it is not mixed with them; ninth, it ceases slander;
tenth, it constantly abides in samādhi. In reality, it does not eat. This city is twelve hundred yojanas in length and breadth, containing nine hundred million households.
To the south is the city wall, and to the north is the vihāra, located in the east. Because it enters from the outside to reach [the interior], it is said that it "enters."
When eating, he eats according to the Dharma; sentient beings possess this superior wisdom, and as the conditions for its awakening are about to arise, it serves to manifest *prajñā*.
His wearing of robes represents being clad in the armor of great vows; his compassionate heart is the holding of the bowl.

The bowl’s ability to contain rice represents practice (*pratipatti*), which is able to approach the principle; it thus symbolizes the city of liberation—the city of the *dharmatā*-nirvāṇa. He contemplates the five...
The huts of the *skandhas* are entirely empty, still, and motionless like a city, representing the *dharmakāya*.
He begs for food in sequence, not bypassing the poor to go to the wealthy, nor abandoning the noble to follow the lowly;

because his great compassion is impartial, this represents the Bodhisattva’s sequential practice, sequential training, and sequential path. Because the causal practices have been perfected, he returns to his original place.

This very place is the locus of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Contemplating sequentially through form and mind until reaching omniscience—picking up the alms bowl, gathering the robes, and washing the feet—is precisely (in one version, "symbolizes") the state after fruition, where there are no longer further vows or practices, and no oaths;

thus the robes are gathered because there is no further progress, and the bowl is taken up because both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are free from further defilement and burden.
Because the sands of ignorance have been forever removed and the water of the Dharma is pure, it is said that he "washes his feet and spreads his seat.
That which serves as the seat is the emptiness of all phenomena; this place of the four fearlessnesses refers to Prajñāpāramitā. The separate introduction is concluded.
At that time, the Elder Subhūti rose from his seat amidst the great assembly;
he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "It is rare, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata skillfully protects and sustains all bodhisattvas, and skillfully entrusts all bodhisattvas."

The Elder Subhūti possesses the virtue of being a leader among men. Just as a divine bell (or "great bell," according to another reading), though resonant, does not ring without being struck, so too the Sage does not respond in isolation;
shadow and echo depend solely upon the benevolent one. Subhūti is also known as Śūnyatā-utpāda (Born from Emptiness) or Śobhita (Well-Auspicious).
Alternatively, it is said that he is the Buddha Śikhin of the East, the Azure Dragon. He rose from his seat to request instruction.
Regarding these rituals, when requesting instruction, one should stand to the side and withdraw from one’s seat;

as for baring the right shoulder, this follows the national custom of regarding such exposure as a mark of respect, while also demonstrating that it is convenient for the disciple to perform the practice. Placing the right knee on the ground and bowing down in a crouched posture signifies an appearance of non-resistance;
joining the palms and assuming a composed, reverent demeanor manifests the gravity of the teacher and the importance of the Way, thereby ensuring the utmost respect.
With the utmost reverence and single-minded devotion, he addressed the Buddha, recounting and praising his rarity:

"From the time of the previous eighty-four thousand years when you held the rank of a Wheel-Turning King until your current existence as Śākyamuni, had you not left the household life, you would have become a Golden-Wheel King for two thousand five hundred years.
That you were able to renounce that throne and beg for alms at the gate is truly rare."

This praises the secret protection of the body, the secret entrustment of the mind, and the secret protection of the speech. Furthermore, it describes the praise found in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
the mental protection and mindfulness is the true path of Prajñā, like a mother who can protect and care for one;
the entrustment is the provisional path of skillful means (*upāya*), like a father who can instruct and guide.
World-Honored One, when good sons and good daughters resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they retrace the aforementioned points to further raise this present inquiry.
"Resolving upon bodhicitta" refers to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*); it is a general indication of the ultimate goal.
Translating [the Sanskrit] as "unsurpassed, right, universal knowledge and awakening," it signifies setting one's mind toward and aspiring for the distant goal of perfect enlightenment.
How should one abide?
Entering into the wisdom of principle (prajñā) is called "abiding"; this is precisely true knowledge (bhūta-jñāna).
How does one subdue the mind?
Skillful means (*upāya*) is expedient wisdom (*prajñā*). As Sudhana said: "I have already set my mind on Bodhi; how should I practice?
How should I study the Way? The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is as you have said. The Tathāgata skillfully protects and sustains all bodhisattvas."
The Buddha has entrusted the Bodhisattvas well.
The ritual for praise and invitation as you have described it accords with principle and adapts to the capacities of beings; it is truly excellent and perfect, just as you have said.

Listen attentively now, and I shall explain for you how a son or daughter of good family who has resolved their mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should abide and how they should subdue their mind.
"If one does not listen with careful scrutiny, one will leak words and lose the principle; therefore, I admonish you to listen attentively, for the words and principles shall not be in vain.
"So be it, World-Honored One; we wish and desire to hear them.
This expresses respectful compliance with the compassionate admonition to speak, as the mind is inclined with solemn reverence.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should subdue their minds in this way:
'Whatever classes of sentient beings there may be—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation;
whether possessing form or formless; whether possessing perception, lacking perception, or neither possessing nor lacking perception.'"

Regarding the subduing of the mind, this concerns the vow; regarding the abiding of the mind, this concerns practice. Both are characterized by non-existence, serving as the cause for the signless (*animitta*).

The Dharma-body is formless, serving as the fruit of non-attainment (*anupalambha*). In the question, one first abides and subsequently subdues; in the answer, one first subdues and subsequently abides.

This is because, in relation to the arousal of the mind, the vow comes first and the practice later. Having extensively made great vows to provisionally guide [beings] beforehand, one subsequently enters the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*).

By abiding in the dharma of non-abiding, one dwells in the sublime principle. If we consider the essentials of practice, one must first cultivate true wisdom (*prajñā*) and subsequently employ the provisional path (*upāya*);

thus, there are two contemplations in sequence: first abiding, then descending. However, when it comes to the time of realization, the provisional and the real are awakened within a single mind, no longer having a temporal succession.
Now, regarding the stage of the vow, there are four [aspects], the first of which is "extensive and great."

First is the threefold constant mind, and fourth is the non-perverted mind. Regarding the first, the vast mind: the Bodhisattva makes a vow to universally rescue all things because it is boundless and far-reaching;
thus it spans horizontally across the four modes of birth and extends vertically through the three realms.

These four modes of birth are that which dwell within the three realms, serving as the basis for what is dwelt upon. "Egg" refers to that which contains and stores [the embryo]; "womb" refers to that which is nurtured by moisture; "moisture" refers to that which is sustained by humidity.
Suddenly appearing, he said: "If there is form, it is either the realm of desire or the realm of form;

if there is no form, it is the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which is the highest heaven."
I shall cause all beings to enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and bring them to final liberation.
Because it bestows the ultimate bliss of the quiescence of *nirvāṇa*, it is called "the foremost. Phenomena do not arise of themselves; they arise due to causes and conditions.

Yet, the self-nature (*svabhāva*) of these causes and conditions is entirely empty. To accord with this principle is liberation; to deviate from this fundamental truth constitutes delusion. Delusion...

To immediately realize that the cycle of birth and death involves the suffering of body and mind, and that upon this realization, burdens are extinguished, suffering ends, and one abides in stillness and eternal bliss—this is called *nirvāṇa* (extinction).
In the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), *nirvāṇa* refers to the extinction of the physical form and the cessation of consciousness, which is termed "without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*).

In the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*), it is termed "without remainder" because there are no burdens that are not exhausted and no virtues that are not perfected. When the contemplation of arising and ceasing remains within the realm of names and designations, it is termed "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*).
Thus, although one brings immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings to extinction, in reality there are no sentient beings who attain extinction.
If there were subject and object, one would become weary; because there is no weariness, it is called the "constant mind" that delivers immeasurable and boundless [beings].
Regarding the ultimate non-existence of those to be saved, the "Chapter on Emptiness" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "To save sentient beings is like saving empty space;
it clarifies that not even a hair’s breadth of a sentient being can be apprehended. To understand that sentient beings are fundamentally non-existent is itself awakening;
awakening is what is called "saving. If there were any sentient beings to be saved, Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others would incur the sin of killing.
From the perspective of the principle of a single body, in reality there are no sentient beings; it is only through the delusion of sentient beings that they falsely cling to their existence.
Now, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, out of compassion, teach the Dharma so that they may realize this original non-existence. This realization is called "deliverance.
In truth, there are no distinct sentient beings who exist apart from this principle and are delivered while remaining attached to nirvana.
Why is this? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva possesses the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of a life-span, they are not a bodhisattva.

Because realization is attained through the relinquishing [of such notions], if there were a self or a person, one could speak of their cessation; however, these are merely conventional designations, falsely imputed by people.
To hold to the self is wrong, while to forget the self is right; once this distinction between right and wrong is revealed, gain and loss become clear.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* fully elucidates the sixteen views: first, the view of a self (*ātman*); second, a sentient being (*sattva*); third, a life-span (*jīva*); fourth, a nourisher (*poṣa*); fifth, one who is born (*jantu*);
sixth, a nurturer (*puruṣa*); seventh, a person (*pudgala*); eighth, a human (*manuja*); ninth, an agent (*kāraka*); tenth, one who causes to act (*kārāpaka*); eleventh... [and so forth].
The "ariser" refers to the twelve underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*); the "ariser" [in another sense] refers to the thirteen; the "experiencer" refers to the fourteen underlying tendencies;
the "experiencer" [in another sense] refers to the fifteen; the "knower" refers to the sixteen; and the "viewer" refers to this—here, only four are briefly explained.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice giving without dwelling on any phenomenon;
that is to say, one should not dwell on form when practicing giving, nor should one dwell on sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena when practicing giving.

To practice giving while relying on the foundation of non-abiding is precisely to abide in Prajñāpāramitā. In this Sahā world, it is appropriate to employ the meaning of *dāna* (giving) to subsume all six perfections:
material giving subsumes [the perfection of] giving; the giving of fearlessness subsumes [the perfections of] morality and patience;

and the giving of the Dharma subsumes the final three. By citing only the single term *dāna*, all six are thereby included. A mind that relinquishes without stinginess is called giving; there is no mark (*nimitta*) that can be maintained therein.
What stinginess could there be? Giving is the foremost of the six perfections; dust is the catalyst for the arising of dharmas.
Since both of these dharmas are empty, how could anything not be exhausted?
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should give in this manner, not dwelling on signs. Why is this? If a bodhisattva...
The merit of practicing giving without dwelling on signs is inconceivable and immeasurable.
That neither the giver nor the recipient can be apprehended is precisely what constitutes "not dwelling on signs. Because one gives with an empty mind, the merit is immeasurable;
since the principle is thus limitless, the mind should not be restricted. When one practices giving in accordance with this principle, the resulting merit becomes even more vast.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Can the space of the eastern direction be measured? No, World-Honored One.
Subhūti, can the space of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir be measured? No, World-Honored One.
Subhūti, the merit of a bodhisattva’s giving without dwelling on signs is likewise inconceivable."
As for the measure:
since the principle and the practice have been revealed, if one acts according to what has been taught, the merit will be exceedingly great, equal to the vast void.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should simply abide as instructed.
The words of the Sage are without error and their principles cannot be transgressed; as the Buddha has taught, one should settle the mind and abide in the true reality (*dharmatā*).
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of physical marks?
The vows and practices take non-characteristic (*animitta*) as their cause; the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), being formless, takes non-attainment as its fruit.

The Bodhisattva’s generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*) has three meanings: first, to transform sentient beings; second, to cultivate the myriad practices (*sarvacaryā*); and third, to head toward Bodhi.

"Subduing" clarifies the transformation of beings, while "distinguishing the abodes" demonstrates the cultivation of practice. The physical marks of the Tathāgata’s body are the essence of the fruit of Bodhi; if one realizes the Dharma-body, [the marks are understood].
If one thinks that Bodhi can be attained by calculating the nature [of reality] as substantial, one is far removed from it; this passage cites the Dharmakāya to clarify that Bodhi is empty.
"No, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of physical marks. Why is this? Because that which the Tathāgata has taught..."
The physical marks are themselves not physical marks.
Subhūti, having deeply realized the Dharma-body, said that one cannot see it by means of physical marks.

Whether one speaks of one body and one wisdom, or of the true and the responsive bodies, or of the dharma, reward, and responsive bodies—all these clarify the fruit; yet when one reaches the principle of the fruit, [they are no longer so].
The arising of non-arising is the principle of *prajñā*, yet this non-arising of non-arising is the *dharmakāya* and is ineffable.

The non-arising of non-arising of the two fruits of habituation and retribution is the *saṃbhogakāya* and is ineffable. The non-arising of non-arising of compassionate vows is the *nirmāṇakāya* and is ineffable.
Since these three bodies are all ineffable, how can one grasp them by means of physical marks?
One sees the Tathāgata through causes and conditions; if those who have attained the Way hear this teaching, they immediately awaken and see the Tathāgata.
If one hears it and does not awaken, then although the physical marks are described, they are in fact not physical marks, and therefore cannot be seen.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "All that has marks is entirely empty and false. If one perceives all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata.
It is neither cause nor effect; yet because there are causes and conditions, one may speak of it as a cause and may also speak of it as an effect, just as [the beginning] is not the first."
The flame is not a subsequent flame, yet it is not separate from the initial and subsequent flames; this is precisely the meaning [of the teaching].

Now, to take characteristics as non-characteristics does not mean that one eliminates characteristics to find a separate "non-characteristic" elsewhere. If one can act in this way, one will see the Tathāgata.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, will there be any sentient beings who, upon hearing such spoken words and phrases, will give rise to true faith?
The Buddha told Subhūti, “Do not speak thus. After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during the final five hundred years, there will be those who uphold the precepts.”
Subhūti, you should know that those who cultivate merit and are able to give rise to faith in these words and take them as true,
are people who have planted roots of goodness not under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas, but have already planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable thousands of millions of Buddhas—
those who, upon hearing these words, give rise to pure faith for even a single thought-moment.
The Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees that these sentient beings shall obtain such immeasurable merit.
It is not those who have accumulated [merit] under only one, two, or many Buddhas who can believe this sutra;

rather, it is those who go forth from home and uphold the precepts, or practice for merit while remaining in the secular world during the final five hundred years—ranging from the sixth to the thousandth year, or as it is also said, beginning from the very last five hundred years.
Those who are able to give rise to faith upon hearing the name of the Buddha-dharma have not encountered only one or two Buddhas;

rather, it should be understood that this is their time of attaining the Way following the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, as in the case of the因缘 (nidāna) of Upagupta. If one traces its origin, it is not due to only one or two Buddhas.
Pure faith is the faith of non-attainment (*anupalambha*). That which is signless (*animitta*) constitutes pure faith for the five hundred [arhats].
The Master of Treatises is not one who fails to uphold the precepts or lacks faith in the Mahāyāna; because he has long cultivated the four reliances, he is able to believe.
Having attained pure faith in the true mark (*dharmatā*), the Tathāgata knows him with his knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) and sees him with his Buddha-eye.
Seeing that a single moment of pure faith gains immeasurable merit, it is like one person offering flowers to the Buddha themselves, while another person offers flowers [to someone else].
Regarding the merit obtained from making offerings to the Buddha for others: when asked by an Arhat, he could not see it; when asked by Maitreya, Maitreya replied:
"One who has exhausted suffering for oneself becomes a Pratyekabuddha, while one who does so for others attains Buddhahood; this is because of the Bodhisattva-mind.

Thus, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, and Prajñā, are the mother of the Buddhas. The Buddha constantly observes with his eye this sutra and those who receive and uphold it; their merit is immeasurable.
It is equal to empty space and cannot be fathomed by those of inferior capacity; only a Buddha can know and see it.
Why is this? Because these sentient beings no longer possess the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a being, or the notion of a life-span.
"I" refers to the person as the subject; "self" refers to sentient beings as the objects of perception; "life-force" serves to connect with what precedes; and "soul" serves to link with what follows.
These four are collectively termed "clinging to a person," established according to their specific applications and given four names.
In detail, they comprise sixteen types of views. To cling to these views and not believe in Prajñā is [the fault].
There is no mark of dharmas, nor is there any mark of non-dharmas.

What is now called "dharma" refers to the emptiness of the five aggregates as dharma, and the marks of the five aggregates as non-dharma. Taking the emptiness of the aggregates as medicine is called dharma;
the existence of the aggregates as a sickness is called non-dharma. Once the sickness of the aggregates has been eliminated, the medicine of emptiness is also discarded.
When the unrighteous has already departed, the righteous likewise perishes. Furthermore, maintaining the precepts constitutes the righteous, while violating them constitutes the unrighteous.
Next, if one either maintains or violates them, both are unrighteous; that which is neither maintaining nor violating is the righteous—this is the meaning of the Middle Way.
Only when one’s faith penetrates this Middle Way and departs from the two extremes of existence and non-existence does one truly believe in this sutra.
Why is this? If these sentient beings take up signs with their minds, they immediately become attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.

If they take up the signs of dharmas, they likewise become attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span. Why is this? If they take up the signs of non-dharmas, they too become attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
Therefore, you should not grasp at the Dharma, nor should you grasp at what is not the Dharma.
For this reason, the Tathāgata has always said to you, bhikṣus: "Understand my teaching of the Dharma as being like a raft;
even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not the Dharma."
It is like one who wishes to cross a river and constructs a raft to carry themselves across; once they have reached the other shore, they abandon the raft and depart.

To transcend birth and death, one temporarily relies upon the myriad practices; once nirvana is attained, all wholesome deeds are likewise relinquished. If even the Dharma must be relinquished, how much more so that which is not the Dharma?
Initially, one abandons evil through goodness; ultimately, both are abandoned.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Or has the Tathāgata preached any dharma?
Subhūti replied, “As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no fixed dharma that is called ‘anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.’”
In *samyaksambodhi*, there is likewise no fixed dharma that a Tathāgata can speak of.

That which is without fixity is the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*); when characteristics are exhausted and fully understood, it is called bodhi. Because it is signless (*animitta*), it does not exist; because it is a provisional name, it is not non-existent.
Since it is neither existent nor non-existent, what reality could be attained, and what fixed dharma could be spoken? This is the response through transformation.

The Nirmāṇakāya is neither the true Buddha nor the speaker of the Dharma; yet, while the true [Buddha] does not speak, the same applies to the response-body (nirmāṇakāya). Apart from the true, there is no response-body;
the response-body is not different from what has come down from the beginning. The true [Buddha] does not speak, yet the response-body speaks. Speaking is non-speaking; non-speaking is speaking.
If one knows that the Tathāgata is eternally non-speaking, this is called being fully endowed with much learning (bahuśruta).
Why is this? Because all the dharmas taught by the Tathāgata are ungraspable and ineffable; they are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas.
Why is this so? It is because all worthy ones and sages are distinguished from one another by means of the dharma of unconditionedness (*asaṃskṛta*).
All phenomena are empty and ineffable; they are not "dharmas" in the sense of existing, nor are they "non-dharmas" in the sense of being non-existent.
This is the ultimate point where both existence and non-existence are transcended. Why is this so? Because the principle is without arising or ceasing, it is called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Regarding this principle of the unconditioned, all the sages have the same understanding. Through this realization of the unconditioned, fetters are exhausted and the Way is perfected; this constitutes the meaning of liberation.
Although they equally enter the unconditioned nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), there are distinctions of clarity and obscurity, as well as depth and shallowness, in their understanding.

Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would the merit obtained by that person be great? Subhūti said: "It would be very great, World-Honored One."
Why is this? This merit is not a substantial merit; therefore, the Tathāgata says that the merit is great.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if there is someone who, from this sutra, receives, upholds, or even recites as little as a four-line verse for others, their merit shall surpass the former.
Why is this? Subhūti, all Buddhas and the unsurpassed... [of all Buddhas]... [arise] from this.
The Dharma of *samyak-saṃbodhi* all issues from this sutra, Subhūti; what is called "Buddha-Dharma" is indeed not Buddha-Dharma.
Previously, space was cited—how could that ever be exhausted? Now, a single moment of faith and understanding is again weighed against it in turn. Accumulated...

"Much treasure yet meager merit" refers to the four lines [of scripture], which are concise yet yield profound blessings. Three thousand pieces of gold and jade serve only to sustain the body; whereas a single verse, though brief, is so wondrous as to nourish the spirit.

Those who cherish the merit of the Buddha—even those at the seventh stage of realization—do not forget this; its subtle manifestation is difficult to perceive, and one ought to respond with a mind of emptiness.
These seven treasures are mundane matters of virtuous conditions; through them, one attains the fruits of rebirth among devas and humans, yet they do not lead to the unshakeable state.

Because it does not emerge, one guides it with the wisdom that emerges through movement, thereby attaining the realization of Bodhi. A single moment of perfect faith can guide all wholesome qualities;

this mind is supreme. The true mark (*dharmatā*) is able to give rise to all phenomena, yet these phenomena are themselves not phenomena—this is the non-arising of all phenomena, which is the arising of Prajñā.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does a stream-enterer have the thought, ‘I have attained the fruit of stream-entry’?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One. Why is this? One is called a stream-enterer because they have entered the stream, yet there is nothing entered.
Because they do not enter forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles, they are called a stream-enterer.”
This is called practicing the untainted (anāsrava), which is both to go against the current of birth and death and to enter the stream of the Path.

Not entering the realm of form is "going against the current. To elaborate: regarding the statement that there is neither going against the current nor entering [the stream] during contemplation, as for "not entering form," this refers to the six sense objects (ṣaḍviṣaya) produced by past ignorance.
Since the ignorance that produces them is not real, how could the six sense objects it produces be real?
Since these [views] are not real, how can one definitively establish their existence or non-existence? One calculates by means of the indeterminate nature;

therefore, it is called "not entering the ocean," for it is merely a river among the many streams. It is the abyss of the ultimate Bodhi-spirit where, first encountering non-arising (*anutpāda*), one must exhaust the source.
In principle, there is no discordance or compliance; what "entering" could there be? Because it violates principle, one enters the six sense-objects and turns one's back on the Truth.
Dust is immediately reconciled with principle; all categories of fruits are likewise so.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can a Sakṛdāgāmin form the thought, "I have attained the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin"?
Subhūti said, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? The name 'Sakṛdāgāmin' means 'one who comes back once more,' yet—"
In reality, there is no coming or going; this is what is called a Sakṛdāgāmin (Once-returner).
This is also called "Abiding in Thinness" because, among the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm, six grades have already been severed while three grades remain;
thus, he is called a "Thin One. Having taken birth once each in the realms of humans and devas, he then becomes an Arhat; therefore, he is called "One who Returns Once."
Although there is coming, in reality there is no one who comes or goes, because they have already attained the two-fold emptiness of birth and dharmas.
Subhūti, what do you think? Does a non-returner (anāgāmin) have the thought, "I have attained the fruit of a non-returner"?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? A non-returner is defined as 'one who does not come back' (an-āgāmin), yet..."
In reality, there is no one who does not come; therefore, they are called Anāgāmin.

This is translated as "Non-returner" (Bùhuán) and also as "One who does not come" (Bùlái). Since their fetters in the Desire Realm are exhausted and they have realized the state of No-more-learning (aśaikṣa) in the higher realms, one should say "non-coming.
The omission of the character "not" (bù) in some instances is merely a stylistic variation in the text.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Can an arhat have the thought, 'I have attained the path of an arhat'?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Because, in truth, there is no dharma named 'arhat.
World-Honored One, if an arhat were to have the thought, 'I have attained the path of an arhat,' that would constitute attachment to a self, a person, a being, and a life."

"Sentient beings and life-span possessors"—this is called "non-attachment" (*asaṅga*) and also "non-arising" (*anutpāda*). Those for whom birth in the three realms has ceased and whose tasks are accomplished are called Arhats.

Among these, the first three are [designated as] the path (*mārga*), while the latter is the fruit (*phala*). Although the reality of the fruit (*phala-tattva*) encompasses all four, it is specifically termed the "path" because one attains both the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*) and non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Because the path of the wise śrāvakas has reached its ultimate limit, it is designated by the name "the path.
The World-Honored One, the Buddha, said: "I am foremost among men in the attainment of the samādhi of non-contention;
I am a first-rate arhat who is free from desire. Yet I do not harbor the thought: "I am an arhat free from desire. World-Honored One, if I...
If he were to think, "I have attained the path of Arhatship," the World-Honored One would not say that Subhūti is one who delights in the practice of araṇā;
for Subhūti actually practices nothing at all, yet he is named Subhūti, one who delights in the practice of araṇā.
Verifying the principle through one's own understanding, it is not false; the mind is empty and eternally tranquil—whence could conflict arise?
*Lana* refers to the characteristic of tranquility: when external activity is exhausted and the internal mind is stilled, both internal and external are simultaneously quiescent.

When is it not tranquil? It is called "not false" because it must correspond to reality. *Lana* is translated here as "non-activity. If one claims for oneself to be free from [disturbance], [it is true].
If desire is itself something that exists, what is meant by "non-existence"?
Subhūti, what do you think? Did the Tathāgata, when he was formerly with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, obtain any dharma?
"No indeed, World-Honored One. When the Tathāgata was with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he truly obtained no dharma whatsoever."
When the Tathāgata was formerly practicing the *Prajñāpāramitā*, he did not merely not enter into provisional names or [the realms of] form, fragrance, and so forth;
he likewise did not enter into *nirvāṇa* nor did he enter into the Middle Way. It is for this reason that he attained *bodhi*.

The four reliances (*catuḥpratisaraṇa*) are clarified up to this point, showing how a person who possesses faith in a single thought-moment subdues their mind and realizes the signlessness of non-self (*anātman*).
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does a bodhisattva adorn buddha-fields? "No, World-Honored One. "And why is that?
That which is called 'adorning a buddha-field' is not actually adorning; it is merely named 'adorning.
Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to a pure mind in this way: they should not give rise to a mind by dwelling upon form."
When the mind arises in response to sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and dharmas, it should arise without abiding anywhere.
To realize this single thought of pure faith is to discern its proper mode of abiding: to abide in *prajñā* by means of non-abiding and thereby take hold of a Buddha-land.
This constitutes the four kinds of adornment; if one’s own adornment is pure, this is the Land of Quiescent Light (*śāntaprabhā*). As for the discussion of transformation...
He is endowed with the characteristics of the four lands: when delusion prevails, the land is defiled; when emptiness and luminosity prevail, the land is pure and adorned.

The meaning of adorning the land likewise lies in the empty mind. To thus adorn and purify the land, one should practice *dāna* and other perfections to give rise to a pure mind that does not dwell on form or fragrance.
This mind has no dwelling—through these three stages of dharma, non-dharma, and so forth—a single thought of purity is the state of non-dwelling.
To abide is to abide by means of that which is non-causal, and so forth.
Subhūti, suppose there were a person whose body was like Sumeru, the king of mountains; what do you think, Subhūti? Would that body be large? Subhūti replied:
"It would be very large, World-Honored One. Why is this? Because the Buddha has taught that what is not a body is called 'large'."
Body. This is not a fruit, yet it is a fruit; Sumeru, translated as "Peaceful Brilliance" (Anming), is composed of four precious substances.

Among the ten mountain ranges, there are: first, the Snowy Mountains; second, the Fragrant Mountains; third, Mount Kailāsa; fourth, the Mountain of Seers and Sages; fifth, the Mountain of... [text truncated]

1. Gandhamādana Mountain; 2. Ṣaḍaśīrṣa Mountain; 3. Nimindhara Mountain; 4. Cakravāḍa Mountain; 5. Yugandhara Mountain; 6. Aśvakarṇa Mountain; 7. Vinataka Mountain; 8. Īṣādhara Mountain; 9. Sumeru Mountain.
Because the cause is great, the fruit is great; having attained the *dharmatā*, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) accomplish the *dharmakāya*.
Thus they are called "great," like Sumeru. Sumeru is used as a metaphor for *dharmatā*; because form (*rūpa*) is great, it is called "Panna" (Perfection).
If the mountain is great, the great deity is also great; since the fruit of cultivation is perfected, the retributive fruit is also fulfilled.
Because the Dharma-body is not a physical body, it is called the "Great Body.
Subhūti, suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—what do you think? [Would those be many?]
"How many would all those Ganges rivers be? Would they not be many? Subhūti replied, "They would be very many, World-Honored One;
even the Ganges rivers alone would be countless, let alone their sands. Subhūti, I now tell you truly:
if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who filled as many great trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in all those Ganges rivers with the seven treasures...
“Would one obtain much merit by giving away a thousand worlds as a gift? Subhūti replied, “Very much, World-Honored One.

The Buddha told Subhūti, “If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, from within this sutra, were to even accept and uphold a four-line verse or the like and explain it for others, the merit from this would surpass the former merit.”
The Ganges is the name of a deity; this river is eight thousand *yojanas* long and four thousand *yojanas* wide.

It is so deep that even elephants sink when crossing it, and its sand is as fine as flour. Its water is white like milk. The initial mention of "three thousand" does not refer immediately to the Ganges itself;
rather, starting from a small number and proceeding to a large one, a single Ganges serves as the basis, and then the sands of all such Ganges rivers are counted.

Regarding the threefold numerical comparison where giving away many jewels yields little merit while upholding even a small portion of this sutra yields great merit—this is due to the superior efficacy of the sutra;
therefore, it is said that "this merit surpasses the former merit."
Furthermore, Subhūti, wherever this sutra is spoken, even as little as a single four-line verse, you should know that this place should be honored by all the world—
including its devas, humans, and asuras— as if it were a stupa or temple of the Buddha; how much more so for anyone who can fully receive, uphold, read, and recite it.
Throughout all worlds, the places where the teachings were expounded are honored by gods, humans, and asuras alike; they are briefly described as the three wholesome paths of existence.

These places are venerated like stupas—here called *fangfen* (square mounds) or *lingmiao* (spiritual temples)—because they are the honored *dharmakāya*. Thus, the stupa is held in high esteem because it is the site where the sutra was preached.

Regarding the value of the location where the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* was taught, the construction of a stupa for the *śarīra* (relics) does not equal that of the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Why? Because it was the place where [the teaching] was spoken.
Just as with a stūpa, the meaning is indeed so; however, because worldly people revere stūpas, the place where [this teaching] is spoken is treated like a stūpa.
Subhūti, you should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme, foremost, and rare dharma.

Because the Dharma is subtle and its principles are praised by people, it is fitting that it should be so; this rare Dharma is the accomplishment of Bodhi, and thus the person [who realizes it] is worthy of veneration.
As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the "most real matter" is precisely the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the supreme Dharma.
Wherever this sūtra resides, there is a Buddha or a respected disciple. If a person can propagate the Dharma, then the person possesses the Dharma;
if the Dharma completes the person, then the Dharma possesses the person. The principles governing the relationship between person and Dharma should be held in high esteem.
If the fruition is not yet realized but is being realized, then there is a Buddha; if the cause is not yet established but is being established, then [there is a Buddha].
The honored disciples referred to are Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, and others.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what should this sutra be named? How should we uphold it?"
"Practicing in accordance with it is 'receiving,' and propagating it extensively is 'upholding. To establish these three as a model for practice, I ask about its method.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "This sutra is named the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. By this name, you should receive and uphold it."

The meaning of the title has already been fully established. Since the objective realm (*ālambana*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) follow one another, they are collectively termed *prajñā*. However, it is essential to distinguish them specifically;

[wisdom] ultimately resides within the noble mind (*ārya-citta*). By grasping the main principles and raising the subordinate details, the terminology is aligned with its meaning, and through the name, the correct principle is revealed; thus, it is appropriate that this be cultivated.
Why is this so? Subhūti, that which the Buddha calls the *prajñāpāramitā* is not, in fact, the *prajñāpāramitā*.
For names are not established in vain; they must correspond to their reality. Just as nothing can withstand being struck by a diamond without being shattered, so too is this wisdom.

That which is illuminated—the dharmas—has nothing that is not empty; this is precisely what is meant by "non-Prajñā" and "the emptiness of wisdom. When the object is extinguished and wisdom is forgotten, what characteristic would not be exhausted?
The profound intent of upholding [this teaching] should lie herein. In this commentary, first there is "nothing whatsoever," and second there is also "nothing whatsoever";
yet because their meanings differ, it clarifies that it is not "not-anything-at-all. This distinguishes the meaning of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (prakṛti-śūnyatā). First:

"Nature is itself empty" refers to the second [type of emptiness], which refutes nature by explaining emptiness: that which existed previously is non-existent, and that which was subsequently absent is non-existent.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "All dharmas are non-existent; such is their existence, and such is their non-existence. Not knowing this matter is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
Regarding "existence" being non-existent, it is in relation to what preceded; regarding "non-existence," it is in relation to what followed. This is the teaching of the Tripiṭaka masters.
The explanations of the meaning of "nature" (*svabhāva*) set forth in the middle [turning] all belong to the refutation of nature and are subsumed under the teaching of emptiness;
for while this nature was previously held to exist as a condition, it is now entirely non-existent. Thus, it is said that what existed has become non-existent.
This statement of non-existence, when contrasted with the subsequent clarification that all phenomena are non-existent yet possess the sense of not being non-existent, elucidates the meaning.

Thus, because it exists, the Sūtra says that not knowing is called ignorance (*avidyā*). To refute its substantial nature by speaking of the emptiness of nature is a horizontal discourse on the disease of refutation;
all such [views] are thoroughly cleansed. This "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*) is both exhaustion and purity (*śuddhi*), and this purity is also purity.

A vertical discourse concerns entering the Path; although there is exhaustion, there is also a sense of non-exhaustion. This is discussed in relation to the Path, wherein this very exhaustion and purity constitute the Path, and the Path exists.
The functions of transforming the profane into the sacred differ; while there is nothing such as "two heads" or "three hands," there is nevertheless the meaning of "not non-existent.

This is precisely the meaning of "thus existent. If, in the former case, "non-existent" refers to a state of absolute non-existence where even non-existence itself is non-existent, then the latter clarification of "non-existence" means that it is, in fact, not non-existent.

Although the names "all" and "non-existent" are the same, their meanings differ. Within the preceding section, the first clarifies that which is like emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and the second clarifies that which is like non-emptiness.
Why is this so? The Buddha taught that *prajñāpāramitā* is precisely not *prajñāpāramitā*; this is what is meant by being like emptiness.

Since one takes the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) as *prajñā*, and *prajñā* is precisely not [inherently existent] *prajñā*, the emptiness of intrinsic nature is likewise [like emptiness].
"Emptiness.
Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata preached any Dharma? Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has not preached anything."
When both object and wisdom are empty, what further can be said? Whether one speaks or does not speak, both are as they are;
both forms of knowledge are empty. Subhūti, what do you think? Are all the atoms contained within a trichiliocosm many?
Subhūti replied: "Very many, World-Honored One. Subhūti, those atoms spoken of by the Tathāgata are, in fact, not atoms.
"Dust" refers to subtle particles; the Tathāgata says that what is called a "world" is not a world, yet it is called a world.
Because these subtle particles are not actually subtle particles, they are called subtle particles; thus, they are non-existent. In this manner, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"Not knowing [the nature of things] is called ignorance (*avidyā*). To now clearly understand this "existence as such" is itself wisdom. [This is the meaning of] "dispersing."
If the world were composed of atoms, since the world has no intrinsic nature, it would not be the case that what is merely a provisional name is itself [the reality].
