Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks? "No, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has said that the thirty-two...
These two marks are themselves non-marks; this is called the thirty-two marks.
These non-marks are merely provisional names for bodily characteristics. It is simply that the body is taken as "non-body";

it is not that the body is eliminated and there exists a separate "non-body," nor is it that the marks are eliminated and there exists a separate "marklessness. Marks and marklessness are neither identical nor different.
Subhūti, if there were good sons or good daughters who were to give away their lives as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River in acts of charity,
and if there were another person who, from within this sutra, were to receive, uphold, or even recite as little as a four-line verse for the sake of others,
the latter’s merit would be far greater.

Having stated the name of the sutra, there is another round of comparative evaluation: by first entrusting the relinquishing of wealth to clarify its superiority, and now entrusting the relinquishing of the body to demonstrate its greater magnitude—wherein the *upabhoga* (enjoyment-retribution) is easy to abandon while the *ātmabhāva* (personal-retribution) is difficult to discard—this shows the gradual nature of the transformation from the easier to the more difficult.

Even through the giving of one's body and life, one cannot avoid rebirth; yet through the propagation and upholding of the four lines [of the verse], the afflictions are extinguished and the Path is accomplished.
At that time, having heard this sutra being preached, Subhūti deeply understood its meaning and intent; he wept with tears of sorrow and said to the Buddha:

"It is rare, World-Honored One! Regarding such a profound sutra as this preached by the Buddha, from my past until now, though I have attained the eye of wisdom, I have never before heard a sutra such as this."
Alas! I lament my late awakening and grieve for those who have not yet heard [this teaching], out of compassion for all sentient beings who do not know this Dharma;

I grieve because I have heard it and rejoice; I grieve with deep sorrow for those of the Hīnayāna; alas, I grieve because I reproach myself for failing to contemplate emptiness properly and thus claiming to have attained the eye of wisdom;
although I had heard [of such things] previously, I had not yet heard that one should subdue [the mind] in this manner.
It abides. World-Honored One, if there should be anyone who hears this sutra and their faith becomes pure, they will then give rise to the mark of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
You should know, World-Honored One, that such a person accomplishes the foremost and most rare merit. World-Honored One, this mark of reality is itself no-mark.
For this reason, the Tathāgata speaks of it as the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
The true mark is precisely the absence of marks; if there were even the slightest mark, it would not be the true mark.
Therefore, the Tathāgata declares that the absence of marks is the true mark. If a person can believe this, is it not the foremost rarity? Yet he says they have "arisen."
The true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is precisely the arising of non-arising. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Because form does not arise, the prajñāpāramitā arises.
If one understands that form is non-arising, then the wisdom of the contemplation of non-arising is produced; therefore, prajñā arises.
“World-Honored One, for me now to hear such a sutra as this and to believe, understand, accept, and uphold it is not difficult.

But what would be difficult about believing it only after one has transcended the Buddha-way and attained realization of the holy state? It is easy to believe because one has encountered the age of a Buddha and personally attained understanding and awakening.”

If, in a future age during the final five hundred years, there should be sentient beings who hear this sutra and believe, understand, accept, and uphold it, such persons would be the most rare and extraordinary.
To be born when not encountering a Buddha and yet be able to believe in such a signless Dharma—is this not indeed difficult? Therefore, [it is said] at the end...
Faith at the time of the Dharma is most worthy of praise.
Why is this? Because such a person lacks the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, and the mark of a life-span.
By virtue of lacking these marks of self, they are able to believe in this sutra; were there even the slightest trace of the marks of self, person, and so forth, they would not.
It is faith. Why is this?
Because the mark of a self is itself no mark; the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, and the mark of a life-span are themselves no marks.
The mark of a self (*ātman*) is precisely no-mark (*animitta*), for not even a fragment of a mark can be apprehended;
since the notions of self, person, and so forth have not possessed even a single mark from the very beginning, their essence is primordially without marks—this itself is marvelous.
This is an explanation by way of inversion (*pratiloma*).
Why is this? Because being free from all marks is precisely what is called the Buddhas.
When marks are exhausted and understanding is perfected, that is to be a Buddha; one is able to transcend existence and non-existence and abide eternally in the ultimate. It was also said previously:
"If you see that all marks are no-marks, then you see the Tathāgata."

The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is, so it is. If there should be anyone who, upon hearing this sutra, is not startled, not terrified, and does not fear, you should know that such a person is extremely rare. Why is this?
Subhūti, what the Tathāgata calls the ‘foremost pāramitā’ is not actually a foremost pāramitā; it is designated as the ‘foremost pāramitā.’”
If Subhūti were to speak for himself, his words might be considered indefinite; however, to say that there is no self or person is itself the Buddha.

The Buddha now confirms this, saying, "It is as you have said," and therefore it is not false. Furthermore, initial astonishment is called *jīng* (startle); a timid heart and weak spirit are called *pù* (fear);
and being deeply loathsome toward prior matters is called *wèi* (dread). Moreover, *jīng* refers to the beginning of practice, while *pù* refers to the Two Vehicles.
These non-Buddhists likewise: first, upon hearing the sutra, they are not startled; second, when contemplating its meaning, they are not terrified; and third, when practicing it, they do not fear.
First, it is the foremost among all the *pāramitās*, including *prajñā*; counted from the end, it is also the first.
Subhūti, that which the Tathāgata calls the perfection of patience is not a perfection of patience.
To endure is called "patience" (kṣānti), and to be subjected to injury is called "insult" (kṣati). Since there is neither self nor person, who could inflict injury upon whom?
That which is non-patience is taken as patience, and patience is taken as non-patience; this is the essence of prajñā.

Why is this? Subhūti, when King Kali cut off my limbs and members of my body in the past, at that time I had no perception of a self, no perception of a person, no perception of a sentient being, and no perception of a life-span. Why is this?

Because if, at the time when my body was severed limb by limb in the past, I had possessed a perception of a self, a perception of a person, a perception of a sentient being, or a perception of a life-span...
He gave rise to anger and resentment.
Regarding King Kali—here translated as "Evil-Born"—why would he endure? That which is not [truly] enduring is cited as proof:

there is endurance when there is suffering, and there is no endurance when there is no suffering. Since there is neither self nor person, how could endurance arise through being cut? If there were a self or a person, it would necessarily...
It is clear that one who can remain tranquil despite the arising of anger is manifestly without a self.
Subhūti further recalled that in the past, for five hundred lifetimes, he had been a rishi of patience;
during all those lifetimes, there was no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a sentient being, and no mark of a life-span.
The Bodhisattva knows that the body is non-existent; thus, giving it away is not difficult. If one possessed this [substantial] body, giving it away would be a great hardship.
In the story of Śibi substituting himself for the pigeon, this is a matter recorded within the Tripiṭaka. Previously, patience was explained as having endurance despite suffering;
now, patience is explained as being free from suffering and possessing joy. Because there is compassion, there is no resentment. Because there is no resentment, there is joy.
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should generate the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* while remaining detached from all signs (*nimitta*).

Since this is the very heart of Prajñāpāramitā, one must thoroughly understand it; thus, at the outset, the bodhisattva is exhorted to generate the mind of awakening while remaining detached from signs.
Since the ultimate state consists in the exhaustion of all marks, one should direct the mind toward it by means of forgetting all attachments.
One should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on forms; one should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.
This refers to the previous admonition not to dwell within a mind attached to form, remaining free from all marks, and not dwelling on sounds, fragrances, and so forth.
One should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere; if the mind dwells anywhere, it is not truly dwelling.
Since Prajñā is without marks, what can the mind take as an object and where could it abide? If the mind has an abiding, that is precisely non-abiding;
for the very mark of abiding is the movement of the mind, and thus it is non-abiding.
Therefore, the Buddha said that a bodhisattva’s mind should not abide in form when practicing giving.
It causes one not to dwell upon the six sense objects while practicing giving; this returns to the previously cited thesis to establish the underlying principle:
because there is no dwelling, one should give with a mind of non-attachment—not dwelling on forms, nor possessing material wealth.
Subhūti, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, a bodhisattva should practice giving in this manner.
By practicing giving for the purpose of benefiting others, one does not expect a reward; thus, the benefit will surely be profound.
The Tathāgata has said that all marks are indeed no-marks; he has also said that all sentient beings are indeed not sentient beings.
Citing the Buddha’s teaching as proof, [he said]: "All marks are non-existent; I do not see a giver. I have taught that all marks are...

One should not dwell on signs when giving rise to a mind for practicing generosity; furthermore, it is said that all sentient beings are themselves non-sentient beings, and there is no recipient who is not a sentient being to be transformed and thereby received into liberation.
Subhūti, the Tathāgata is one who speaks the truth, who speaks reality, who speaks according to suchness, who does not speak deceptively, and who does not speak otherwise.

By citing the person who can thus speak as a witness, it is established that this is truly genuine, truly sincere, truly without falsehood, and that suchness must necessarily accord with the principle.
Deception is not distinct from falsehood; rather, it is identical from beginning to end, eternally one, for the words of the Sage are never erroneous. Therefore, you should practice accordingly.
Subhūti, as for the Dharma attained by the Tathāgata, this Dharma is neither real nor unreal.
If one relies on the real as being non-illusory, what "real" could there be to be attained?
If you suspect that my teaching of the Dharma is not [the truth], and that the person who speaks it is also not [the truth], then the Dharma I have realized is simply this: the mind itself.
This realization is neither real nor illusory; having abandoned both, it is characterized by such states as being without arising and without cessation. Therefore, what is spoken is thus.
What has been attained is no empty word.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva dwells with the mind fixed on phenomena while practicing giving, it is like a person entering darkness who sees nothing;
if a bodhisattva practices giving with the mind not dwelling on phenomena, it is like a person with eyes when the sun is shining.
One clearly perceives various forms.

This reveals that abiding in signs is not awakening; it is like wandering at night in darkness. If what was previously mentioned as "attainment" is deemed incorrect, and what is subsequently mentioned as "non-attainment" is deemed correct, then if one practices giving while abiding in dharmas such as form, one cannot perceive all phenomena. If one does not abide in dharmas when practicing...
Generosity is like having eyes; just as the sunlight enables one to see forms without confusion, these three factors constitute non-abiding in signs (*animitta*).
Wisdom-vision is the eye, the realm of principle is the sun, and the various manifestations of the myriad practices are the diverse forms.
Since all phenomena are originally empty, the Bodhisattva observes the mind and further realizes its non-existence; yet, while practicing generosity, this is precisely what is seen.
It should be understood that here, the dharma is presented first followed by the simile; this is merely a direct explanation of the simile.

Subhūti, if in a future age there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who are able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, then the Tathāgata, by means of his Buddha-wisdom, will fully know these people and fully see them all.
One shall attain the accomplishment of immeasurable and boundless merit.
Since the principle and function perceived by the Tathāgata are unerring, it is clear that those of the future should apply themselves with diligent cultivation.
Subhūti, if there are good men or good women who, during the first part of the day, [offer] as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River...

If one were to give away bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges during the midday portion of a day, and again give away bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges during the afternoon portion of that same day—
thus giving away one’s body for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas—

and if there were another person who, upon hearing this sutra, believed it with faith and did not reject it, the merit of the latter would surpass that of the former; how much more so if they were to copy, receive, and uphold it?

If one upholds, reads, recites, and explains it to others, and can have such faith as this, they surpass one who gives away as many lives as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River three times a day—dividing a single day into three parts.
Therefore, it is said that the merit of giving at the beginning, middle, and end of the day is profound and vast. If...
If one gives rise to a mind that does not oppose this sutra, the merit surpasses the previous giving; for while giving has limits, faith is infinite.
How much more so for those who copy, uphold, read, recite, and explain it! To speak merely in terms of faith already yields such results, let alone those who propagate and maintain it.
Subhūti, to speak of it in brief: this sutra possesses inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit.
It answers the question of how that which is non-existent can yet possess such inconceivable qualities; it is able to know the fundamental nature of all dharmas.
That which comes has no existence, yet to regard that non-existence as existence is inconceivable.
This passage consists of ten points: first, the principle of the inconceivable; second, the perfection of the Way; third, the ultimate limit of speech; fourth, the exhaustion of beauty;

fifth, the elevation of the fundamental doctrine; sixth, the accumulation of reality; seventh, the concise expression; eighth, the fact that nothing can fathom it; ninth, the inconceivability of calculation; and tenth, the impossibility of encompassing it.
When measured, it is utterly vast, without limit or boundary; to state the essential point, these three phrases suffice.

The principle and the text are equal and devoid of anything existent; thus, that which is not prajñā is prajñā, and that which is not the characteristic of a body is the characteristic of a body—all of which are inconceivable.
The Tathāgata speaks this for those who have set out upon the Great Vehicle; he speaks this for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle.
If there be any person who can receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain it to others, the Tathāgata fully knows such a person and fully sees such a person;
all shall achieve immeasurable, ineffable, boundless, and inconceivable merit. Such persons as these—
This constitutes bearing the burden of the Tathāgata’s *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
From its very beginning, this sutra is for the Mahāyāna and not for the Three Vehicles; it carries [beings] across boundlessly, which is called the Mahāyāna.
Its excellence surpasses the Three Vehicles, and it is termed the Most Supreme. Were it not for such a person, this would not be a mistaken teaching. It encompasses all.
The Tathāgata named Mahā-vijaya-agratara, who knows and sees all, is the supreme being whose Way is lofty and vast; only a Buddha perceives him.
To shoulder the Bodhi is to ensure it does not fall for a thousand years; this "shouldering" refers to the sense of upholding, circulating, and maintaining [the Dharma] through people.
To carry it on one's back or shoulder is the body that is not a body, yet is the body—the Dharma-body which is neither cause nor fruit.
This refers to the two shoulders.

Why is this? Subhūti, those who delight in inferior dharmas and are attached to the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, or the view of a life-span will be unable to hear, receive, read, recite, or explain this sutra to others.

Those of the three vehicles are incapable of hearing [this teaching] and do not believe or accept it; those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle are attached to the two vehicles; those who cling to a self are ordinary worldlings;
and those who cling to views are non-Buddhists. Because they cannot read or recite it, they have lost the meaning of the *Śālistamba-sūtra*. Therefore, it is inconceivable for ordinary people.
Subhūti, wherever this sutra may be found, it should be honored by all the worlds—gods, humans, and asuras;
you should know that such a place is a stupa. All should pay homage with reverence, circumambulate it, and scatter flowers and incense upon that spot.
Because this ground is the locus of the dharma of non-cognition, it is noble; although words are set aside and meanings cease, this place is always surrounded by devas and nāgas.
Just as the places where emperors reside are honored by all people, so too is this place worshipped by devas and humans;
it is a stūpa, and they pay homage with reverence, scattering incense and flowers.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains, reads, and recites this sutra, yet is treated with contempt by others,
their karmic offenses from previous lives— which would otherwise have caused them to fall into the evil realms— are extinguished by virtue of being so slighted by people in the present life.
It means transforming heavy obstacles into light ones. One who inherently possesses heavy obstacles and studies Prajñā will experience the retribution of past heavy sins as light in the present;
they will merely be slighted by others, while their past heavy sins are immediately extinguished. The arising of sin is due to delusion, whereas merit arises from understanding.
Once merit and understanding have accumulated, then past calamities are extinguished.
"When one shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, this is the bestowal of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).
This means that because accumulated afflictions have been extinguished and liberation has arisen, one is capable of ascending to Bodhi; thus, the Buddha grants the prediction in advance.
Subhūti, I recall that in the past, during immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas before the time of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara,
I encountered eight hundred and forty thousand *koṭi-nayuta* Buddhas, all of whom I served and made offerings to without fail.
If there should be anyone in the future final age who is able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the merit they shall obtain will be even greater than that.
The merit from my offerings to all the Buddhas does not equal even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth, nor ten million billionth part,
nor can it be reached by any calculation or analogy;
the merit obtained by one who clearly upholds this sutra surpasses the practices of the Buddha when he first received [prediction] from Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
One who can now uphold this sutra with a mind that attains nothing through the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) shall obtain merit far superior to mine.

The merit derived from encountering eight hundred and forty trillion nayutas of Buddhas over incalculable eons (asaṃkhyeya) and making offerings to them without fail cannot be compared by calculation to the merit of this mental state;
for when the mind is limited, the blessing is small, but when the mind is vast, the merit is great.
Subhūti, if I were to fully describe the merit obtained by good sons and good daughters who, in the final age at the end of time,
receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, some who hear it would have their minds immediately become deranged and confused, falling into doubt and failing to believe.

When the full account of the merit obtained from upholding this sutra—which is characterized by non-attainment—is told, those of the present age will become frantic and fall into doubt, failing to believe or understand it.
Only those who are sagely and possess vast virtue will surely find it boundless; as for those who are frantic and lack faith, they are insufficient to clarify the Way.
Subhūti, you should know that the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable.

Who could fathom its profound depth of the myriad practices? Because it is through non-attainment and non-existence that there is thus non-existence as its meaning, and because it takes what is not Prajñā to be Prajñā, for this reason the meaning of the sutra is inconceivable.
The karmic retribution is likewise inconceivable.
How could the wondrous fruit of Bodhi be subject to deliberation by the mind? As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* clarifies, from the very first arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment...
Because one attains perfect enlightenment and takes the sentient beings of the atom-like dharma-realm as one’s retinue, it is known that the karmic fruition is inconceivable.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, when sons and daughters of good family resolve upon Anuttara-”
“Regarding the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, how should it abide? How should one subdue that mind?
The Buddha told Subhūti: “Good sons and good daughters who have resolved their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should give rise to this thought:
‘I should bring all sentient beings to final liberation (*parinirvāṇa*); I shall liberate all [sentient beings].’”
Although there are sentient beings, in reality there is not a single sentient being who attains parinirvāṇa.

To distinguish the three types of provisional designations (*prajñapti*) within their essential nature: first, the provisional designation of the recipient (*upādāya-prajñapti*); second, the provisional designation of names (*nāma-prajñapti*); and third, the provisional designation of phenomena (*dharma-prajñapti*).

The "recipient" refers to the person; this person is precisely what possesses the name. Between this person and the name, there are the factors that constitute them. These three provisional designations are thus established.

Regarding the Dharma, how can it be explained by means of the three provisional designations (*prajñapti*)? These three provisional designations are both the establishment of dharmas and the destruction of dharmas.

Since we now wish to clarify "non-existence" (*abhāva*), it is necessary to bring these forward for explanation. If one were to horizontally arrange [the analysis] to refute [specific] afflictions, then in reality there would be only this non-existence;
however, if one discusses it vertically in relation to the Path, then while it is non-existent, it is not non-existent.
All these three provisional [designations] are likewise capable of establishing and capable of refuting [the argument]. Thus concludes the discussion on "provisional existence.
Since it is said that they are "provisionally existent," why would they not exist? First, regarding Śākyamuni, because there was originally nothing to be had, he first clarified what is attained:
he clarified the arousal of the mind, desiring to deliver sentient beings by giving rise to the great vow, "I shall bring about their extinction."
"All sentient beings—truly there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa. This clarifies that the Bodhisattva knows sentient beings as being like an illusion;
what could possibly be extinguished? If there were truly sentient beings to be saved, the *Śāstra* states that the Bodhisattva would incur the sin of killing sentient beings.
Furthermore, in the "Chapter on Illusions" (*Nirmāṇaparivarta*) of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the Buddha said to Subhūti: "All dharmas originally exist [only as such] now..."
"No" [is the answer], which addresses Subhūti’s intention: if sentient beings did not exist originally but exist now, why would it be necessary to console a beginner bodhisattva?
Since they are fundamentally unborn from the beginning, how could they now be extinguished?
Why is this? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva possesses the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of a life-span, then they are not a bodhisattva.
From this, it can be seen that the principle of non-attainment is clearly revealed.
Why is this so? Subhūti, in reality there is no dharma whatsoever that gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Because there is no one who gives rise to the mind, it is known that there is no self; for it is precisely because one falsely conceives of a self that delusions arise, and thus [the path] is not [attained].
"Bodhisattva,
Subhūti, what do you think? Did the Tathāgata obtain any dharma called 'anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi' from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara?"
He then cited his own understanding attained when he received his prediction to confirm his previous statement:
"No, World-Honored One; as I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no dharma by which the Buddha, under Dīpaṃkara Buddha, attained anuttarasamyaksambodhi."
The holy mind is difficult to fathom; its meaning may be inferred through reasoning, yet the attainment of the prediction [of enlightenment] arises from the signless.
Within the signless, there is nothing to be attained.
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is, Subhūti! Truly, there is no dharma by which the Tathāgata has attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
“Samyaksambodhi, Subhūti! If there were any dharma that the Tathāgata had attained as anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then Dīpaṃkara Buddha would not have bestowed upon me this prediction:
‘In a future age, you shall become a buddha named Śākyamuni. Because, in reality, there is no dharma by which one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
For this reason, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara bestowed upon me this prediction, saying: "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni.
The Buddha further explained that as for what you have said, because at the time of the causal stage there was already nothing of its own being, there is nothing to be attained.
Buddha bestowed upon me the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). If one perceives any dharma, that would deviate from enlightenment; how, then, could such a person receive a prediction?

Enlightenment is attained through the non-existence of dharmas. Therefore, when Dīpaṃkara bestowed his prediction upon me, it was because I realized the principle of non-existence; realizing this principle is to turn toward the ultimate, and thus I received the prediction.
Why is this? "Tathāgata" means the suchness (*tathatā*) of all dharmas.

If someone were to say that the Tathāgata has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, Subhūti, in reality there is no dharma that the Buddha has attained as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Subhūti, as for the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* attained by the Tathāgata...
In this regard, there is neither reality nor unreality;

because they are identical to suchness (*tathatā*), there is nothing that exists. The nature of all phenomena is empty, and its principle is without contradiction or difference—this is called "suchness" (*tathatā*).
Because one has realized and understood this suchness to the ultimate degree, one is called a Tathāgata. If anyone were to say that a Tathāgata attains *bodhi*, this...
The speech of worldly people consists of irrational words; in reality, there is no dharma by which one attains Bodhi, for both Buddha and person are non-existent.
Since neither person nor dharma exists, who can attain Bodhi? Within Bodhi, one does not perceive right or wrong.
That which is not real is devoid of right and wrong; that which is empty is devoid of wrong.
Therefore, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are Buddha-dharmas. Subhūti, what are called "all dharmas" are not actually all dharmas;
it is for this reason they are called "all dharmas."
Because the Tathāgata exists within all enumerations, ordinary beings who oppose all dharmas are mistaken, while noble ones who accord with all dharmas are correct;
since correctness is itself awakening, all are the Buddha-dharma.

"Subhūti, it is as if there were a person whose body is tall and large. Subhūti said, "World-Honored One, when the Tathāgata says that a person's body is tall and large, it is for the sake of what is not a large body; it is merely designated as a 'large body.'"
To directly take up the human body as one of the aforementioned phenomena: because it is a provisional construct based on conditions, it is vast and lacks intrinsic nature;
thus, it is not the body. Since that which is not the body is taken as prajñā, how could that which is not the body not be the body?
Subhūti, it is the same for a bodhisattva: if one were to say, "I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa," then that person would not be called a bodhisattva.
Why is this? Subhūti, in reality there is no dharma whatsoever that is named "bodhisattva."
One who seeks to extinguish and deliver sentient beings is not called a Bodhisattva; fundamentally, there are no sentient beings. To perceive sentient beings is a deluded view;
such a person deviates from the Way and is not a Bodhisattva. Why is this? The following passage explains that since the Bodhisattva themselves does not exist, how could there be sentient beings?
Therefore, the Buddha taught that all dharmas are without self, without person, without sentient being, and without life-span.
There is no bodhisattva and no sentient being; in all dharmas, there is absolutely no person and no self.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva should say, "I shall adorn the buddha-fields," he is not to be called a bodhisattva. Why is this?
What the Tathāgata calls 'adornment of the buddha-fields' is, in fact, no adornment; it is merely designated as 'adornment.'
With an open mind one advances in the Way; to adorn the lands and save sentient beings is the practice of saving beings, which is skillful means (*upāya*).
To understand emptiness and signlessness is called wisdom (*prajñā*). If one says, "I am able to adorn the lands and transform sentient beings," this is a view of delusion that opposes the Way;
how could such a person be called a Bodhisattva? When the Tathāgata says that what is not adornment is called adornment, it is because there is no [self-conception].
The explanation of the meaning of abiding through the provisional designation of the response to illumination, while existing within transformation, is thus concluded.

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva has realized non-self and dharmas, and since it is said that all dharmas are non-existent, by what name is one called a "bodhisattva"? Now, in reality, there are no such [dharmas].
The Dharma now states that a bodhisattva possesses only a name; it clarifies here that even this name is non-existent.
Why is this called a "bodhisattva"? Because one penetrates the mark of the selflessness of all dharmas, one is called a "true bodhisattva.
It is for this reason that one is able to penetrate selflessness.
The Tathāgata says that one who is truly a bodhisattva is one who has attained thorough penetration; such a non-deceptive true bodhisattva is called "provisional" [in name].
Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye? "Not so, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata possesses it."
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye? "Not so, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata possesses the divine eye.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the wisdom-eye? "Not so, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata possesses the wisdom-eye.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Dharma-eye? "Not so..."
"Does the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, possess the Dharma-eye? What do you think, Subhūti? Does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha-eye?
"It is not so, Blessed One; the Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye."

The Tathāgata immediately knows and sees all such persons; for although their dharmas are many, they do not exceed the two kinds—merit and wisdom—which take the adornment of the mind as their essence.
Thus, emptiness is fully prepared. Although wisdom is manifold, it does not exceed the five eyes: the old tradition calls them the flesh eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*), which sees within obstructions;
the heavenly eye (*divya-cakṣus*), which sees beyond obstructions; the wisdom eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), which sees the true Dharma; and the Dharma eye (*dharma-cakṣus*), which sees... [the path].
The Buddha-eye of the mundane world perceives both internal and external phenomena; it is said here that there are five [eyes] because they are merely differentiations of a single wisdom.
The *Śāstra* states: "The Dharma-eye knows the dharmas of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and so forth, and is therefore called the Dharma-eye.
Thus, knowing the mundane is termed the Dharma-eye. However, while this section fundamentally clarifies that wisdom is empty, it directly distinguishes the five [eyes].
The eye does not say it is empty; rather, its meaning is revealed in what follows. Since the subsequent wisdom-essence is itself empty, how could the wisdom not be empty?
Later, when the merit is clarified, the preceding wisdom is not thereby rendered non-empty.
Although there is a distinction between the existence of the preceding wisdom and the absence of the subsequent merit, the wisdom itself remains consistent.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Are all the grains of sand in the Ganges River truly grains of sand as the Buddha has described them?
"Not so, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata has described them as grains of sand. "Subhūti, what do you think?
If there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in a single Ganges River, and if there were as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers..."
"Is this not much, is it not very much? The World-Honored One, the Buddha, told Subhūti:
"In all those lands, however many kinds of minds there may be among all sentient beings, the Tathāgata knows them all.
Why is this? The Tathāgata says that all minds are 'non-minds'; they are called 'minds' for that reason. Why is this, Subhūti? Because the past mind cannot..."
One cannot find the present mind, nor can one find the future mind.
To cite examples as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is merely for the purpose of comparing and measuring the grasping of the mind to clarify its emptiness.
When the Tathāgata says that the mind is "not-mind," he uses this "not-mind" precisely as "mind"; this is no different from what was stated previously regarding the illumination by the five eyes.

In principle, there is nothing not fully encompassed; by citing both matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), all objects are exhaustively subsumed. The three periods of time cannot be apprehended, yet that which is called "non-mind" is named "mind.
Why? Because the mind of the three periods of time has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that can be apprehended; it is only from conditions (*pratyaya*) that the mind can arise.

"Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would that person, by reason of this, acquire much merit? "No, World-Honored One;
that person would acquire very great merit by reason of this. "Subhūti, if merit were substantial, the Tathāgata would not say that one 'obtains' it."
Because merit is essentially non-existent, the Tathāgata says that one gains much merit.
If it were clear that merit has substantial reality, then it would be limited; how could it then be "much"? It is because taking what is without merit as merit that it is "much.
Since gold and jade have no inherent nature, they can be accumulated until they fill the three thousand worlds; yet since merit has no substantial reality, it can be bestowed boundlessly.
Furthermore, when the delusion regarding the lack of intrinsic nature in the manifold mind is extinguished, understanding arises.
This concludes the section on the provisional nature of phenomena. Subhūti, what do you think? Can a Buddha be seen by means of a body endowed with physical form?

"No, World-Honored One, a Tathāgata should not be seen by means of a body endowed with physical form. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has spoken of the 'body endowed with physical form' as [not being] a body endowed with physical form."
That which is not the perfection of the physical body is called the perfection of the physical body. Subhūti, what do you think?
Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the perfection of the various marks? "No, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata should not be seen by means of the perfection of the various marks. Why is this?
The Tathāgata says that the perfection of the various marks is itself not a perfection; it is merely called the perfection of the various marks."
The perfection of marks.

As for the form-body (*rūpakāya*), the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is like the moon in the sky, and the form-body is like its reflection in water. The forms of the world have no reality that can be perceived;
if one seeks their fundamental reality, it is precisely the dharma-body. Wisdom is the sovereign of all virtues, and giving is the foremost of all [virtues].

The primary form of its manifestation is the sixteen-foot golden body; specifically, the various marks are called "marks" because they appear according to the needs of beings in this Sahā world—how could they be limited to a single location?
Subhūti, do not think that the Tathāgata has the thought, "I shall preach some dharma"; do not hold such a view.
Consider this: if anyone were to say that the Tathāgata has taught any dharma, they would be slandering me, for they would fail to understand what I have taught.
Subhūti, there is no dharma whatsoever that can be taught; it is called "teaching the dharma" only by way of designation.

The manifestation of the Way’s fulfillment and its response through the preaching of the Dharma to transform beings is sometimes erroneously transmitted as the disparagement of the Sage’s name, which constitutes slandering the Buddha.

Since there is no dharma that can be spoken, this is called "preaching the Dharma. Therefore, when one transmits the intention behind the preaching of the Dharma by saying "there is no preaching," it does not mean a state of silence or non-speech;

rather, it means that while there is no [dharma] to be maintained, there is preaching, and thus the preaching is complete. In this way, there is no fault of contradicting the principles of the Dharma.

At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, will there be any sentient beings in future ages who, upon hearing this Dharma being taught, will give rise to faith?
The Buddha said: "Subhūti, they are not sentient beings, yet they are not non-sentient beings. Why is this?
Subhūti, 'sentient beings, sentient beings'—the Tathāgata has said they are not sentient beings; they are merely designated as such."

Regarding the term "sentient beings" (zhòngshēng): these sixty-two characters are absent in the Qin translation but present in the Wei translation; therefore, they are not explained or categorized in the Tiantai commentary.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, when the Buddha attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, is it that there is nothing to be attained?
The Buddha replied, "The Buddha is a person, and *bodhi* is the Way. Because the Buddha has attained the Way, he speaks it to show it to others; yet he says there is no dharma."
"May it be said that one has not yet definitively attained the Way?
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is, Subhūti. In my *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended; this is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
The exhaustion of all marks and the pervasive emptiness is called bodhi. Since bodhi is markless, what is there to be attained?
This quiescence of non-attainment is the ultimate of the Way.
Furthermore, Subhūti, this Dharma is equal, with no high or low; it is named Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

"Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" (Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment) establishes the meaning of *bodhi*. That among people there is neither noble nor base, and among phenomena there is neither beautiful nor ugly, is the meaning of the equality of *bodhi*.
By practicing all wholesome dharmas while being without a self, without a person, without a sentient being, and without a life-span, one attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti, what are called "wholesome dharmas" by the Tathāgata are said not to be wholesome dharmas;
they are merely designated as "wholesome dharmas."
To cultivate all wholesome deeds without [the concepts of] self or person is the true meaning of cultivation.

Just as a straight form produces a straight shadow and harmonious sounds produce a concordant resonance, if one cultivates the causes while forgetting self and person, the fruitless Bodhi will surely be attained.

As for what is called "wholesome dharma" (*kuśala-dharma*): since there is no "person" at the lower level, how could there be a real "wholesome"? "Wholesome" is a name for being free from evil; "dharma" is...
Regarding the meaning of "upholding the path":

Subhūti, if there were someone who took all the heaps of the seven treasures equal in measure to all the Sumeru kings of mountains within a trichiliocosm and used them as a gift for others, yet another person were to take this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra...

Even if one were to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain to others even as little as a four-line verse, the former merit would not equal a hundredth part of it, nor a thousandth, nor ten-thousandth, nor a hundred-thousandth, nor a billionth; indeed, it cannot be reached by any calculation, analogy, or metaphor.
The accumulation of jewels may be exhausted, but the wondrous understanding [of the Dharma] is inexhaustible; a single verse of the Dharma-treasure surpasses immeasurable worldly treasures.
Subhūti, what do you think? You should not say that the Tathāgata has this thought:
"I shall deliver sentient beings. Subhūti, do not have such a thought. Why? Because in reality, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivers.
If there were any sentient beings whom the Tathāgata had delivered, then the Tathāgata would possess a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
Subhūti, when the Tathāgata says that there is a self, it is not actually a self; yet ordinary people think there is a self.
Subhūti, those who are called "ordinary people" by the Tathāgata are, in fact, not ordinary people.
Because awakening has no attainment as its fruit, it is taught through the forgetting of words; do not say that the Tathāgata perceives sentient beings who can be saved.

If one perceives the existence of sentient beings, that constitutes the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*). What is meant by "Tathāgata"? It is merely spoken of as a provisional name (*prajñapti-nāma*) for "self.
Therefore, it is not a real self. Yet, when ordinary people hear this teaching of a provisional name, they fail to comprehend the intent of the words.
The Tathāgata speaks of a real self, yet it is not that which ordinary beings perceive; because ordinary beings are unreal, they can be transformed and made into Buddhas.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks?

This means that because sentient beings exist who can be transformed into the holy Dharmakāya, and because there are those who may aspire toward the sublime marks [of a Buddha], he asks this question.
Subhūti replied, "It is so, it is so; one should view the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks."
The listener truly thinks that one perceives the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.
The Buddha said, "Subhūti, if one were to perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks, then a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin) would also be the Tathāgata."
He immediately used an upāsaka as an analogy to cause him to understand for himself.
Subhūti said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, as I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should not view the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks."
At that time, the assembly thought it was so, but my understanding was not thus.
Then the World-Honored One spoke in verse: "If one sees me by means of form, or seeks me by means of sound, such a person follows a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata."
Golden countenances fill the eyes but are not forms; the eight musical tones fill the ears but are not sounds. To perceive them as partial or erroneous is delusion;
because of this delusion, one does not see.
Subhūti, if you should think that the Tathāgata attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of physical marks, you would be mistaken.
Subhūti, do not conceive such a thought regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

That which is devoid of functional activity (*kriyā*) is precisely that which possesses the meaning of non-interruption and non-extinction; where there is cause and fruit, everything is perfectly manifest.
This is the functioning of *prajñā* and *upāya*. As the Treatise says: "Because one has attained a portion of the essence of *prajñā*, one dwells in emptiness."
In engaging with the functioning of existence, there is no longer any obstruction; although the meanings of "existence" are many, they do not exceed cause and effect.
Attaining *bodhi* is the fruit. Regarding the two aspects within this fruit, first is the admonition, followed by: "Do not harbor such thoughts"—this is the admonition.
The Tathāgata does not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of the marks of perfection.
Do not say that because all dharmas are entirely non-existent, one attains bodhi not by means of the marks of perfection;
nor do you mean that it does not reside exclusively in form and sound. Because it was previously stated that it is not the case that it is not the bodily marks, it is therefore said to be so.
Subhūti, if you should think that one who has set their mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* speaks of the annihilation and extinction of all phenomena, do not hold such a thought.
I caution you against giving rise to the notion of annihilation, for since [the Truth] is utterly quiescent and extinguished, there is no "Way" that reaches the ten directions.

This does not mean that the Response is non-existent; rather, it is because the Response is exhaustive and yet withdraws that it is not eternal. Because its manifestation follows [conditions], it is not interrupted.
Its essence is unified with the Middle Way, serving as the model for governing all things. To limit this to a single direction—is this not indeed erroneous?
Why is this? It is because those who have resolved their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* do not speak of the characteristic of annihilation or cessation regarding phenomena.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to take the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and offer them as a gift;
Regarding the practice of patience (*kṣānti*), one first compares it with the giving of jewels.

If there is another person who, knowing that all phenomena are without self (*anātman*), achieves patience (*kṣānti*), this bodhisattva surpasses the merit obtained by the former bodhisattva. Why? Subhūti, it is because bodhisattvas do not accept merit.
Because patience is perfected through the transcendence of self-forgetfulness, it is supreme.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, why does a bodhisattva not accept merit? The Buddha replied:
“Subhūti, the merit performed by a bodhisattva should not be clung to; for this reason, it is said that he does not accept merit.”
It is said: "One neither accepts nor does one accept the seeds of retribution; having already named this 'attachment,' how could there arise the false defilements of a self or a person?
Subhūti, if anyone were to say that the Tathāgata comes or goes, sits or lies down, that person..."
Understand the meaning of what I have said. Why is this? A Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere;
therefore, he is called a Tathāgata.
If one says that [the Tathāgata] comes from the true suchness (tathatā) and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), then the Sugata himself and his emanations would go to parinirvāṇa.

All these [explanations] fail to understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught. The Tathāgata is the Lord of the Path’s Shading (mārga-chāyā), the abode of provisional manifestations in the world, and the compassionate parent who nurtures all sentient beings;
by citing these three matters, the general purport is clearly revealed. Because there is neither coming nor going, he is named the Tathāgata.

When understanding reaches its ultimate limit and accords with Suchness (tathatā), the essence has no fixed location, yet as conditions encounter objects, he manifests his arrival. There is no "coming" in this manifestation.
Since that from which they arise has already ceased and become hidden, where could they go?
Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to grind this trichiliocosm into fine dust, what do you think?
Would that multitude of atoms be many? "It would be very many, World-Honored One. For what reason?
If this multitude of atoms were substantially real, the Buddha would not have spoken of it as a "multitude of atoms. Why is this?
The Buddha says that the multitude of atoms is not a multitude of atoms; it is merely designated as a "multitude of atoms."
Because worlds are formed from subtle atoms, there is the conjunction of worlds; because there is the conjunction of worlds, views arise.

When the viewer loses [their true nature], they claim these four types of deluded thoughts exist. To "attain" them is not seeing, yet they take what is not seeing for seeing, and so on, even taking what are not atoms for atoms.

To attain these four is entirely the function of *prajñā*; the atoms, the world, and so forth are the *nirmāṇa-rūpa* (dependent retribution), while the view is the *mukhya-rūpa* (primary retribution). Their conjunction constitutes [the state of delusion].

The passage on the permeation of matter and mind begins from here below; it is the function of pulverizing atoms. Good sons, these are all great practices spoken in common with the Buddha of the *Avataṃsaka*, not regarding atoms as actual dust.
World-Honored One, that which the Tathāgata has spoken of as a trichiliocosm is not a world; it is merely named a "world."
Because atoms are not real, they can be broken down into many; because worlds do not truly exist, they can be formed through provisional designation. Why is this?
If worlds were real, they would be a "unified aggregate" (*piṇḍa-grāha*). The Tathāgata has taught that a unified aggregate is...
"Thus, that which is not a unified whole is called a 'unified whole. Subhūti, a unified whole is ultimately inexpressible;
it is only ordinary people who greedily cling to such things."
Because that which is not a conjunction is treated as a conjunction, it is inexpressible; yet to say again that it is a conjunction is likewise not a conjunction.

Therefore, "conjunction" is spoken of only as a provisional designation (*prajñapti*). Why would it not be a conjunction? Since that which is not a conjunction is taken to be a conjunction, how could there ever be a true conjunction?
The four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) of the Great Sūtra are all inexpressible; however, because there are causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), they may also be spoken of. Now, this too—

There is no actual conjunction; it is merely conventionally described as "conjunction. The *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* both refute conjunction; one should know that there is no conjunction.

What is now spoken of as "conjunction" in this sutra is a conventional description in accordance with worldly usage. Ordinary people are greedily attached to phenomena (*dharma*), not realizing that phenomena are themselves the principle (*tattva*).
Since the principle has no intrinsic existence, phenomena likewise have no intrinsic existence. Why is it not called a "world" (*loka*)? If the world were real, [it would not be empty].
If this existence were truly one, it would necessarily be a unified nature that cannot be divided; yet we merely apply the conventional name "sentient being" to what is one.

Since no such unity can be found, these names are without substantial reality and cannot be spoken of as real. Because of doubt, ordinary people become greedily attached and thus reckon them to be real.
“Subhūti, if someone were to say, ‘The Buddha has taught the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span,’ what do you think, Subhūti?
Would that person understand the meaning of what I have taught? “No, World-Honored One. That person would not understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught.
Why is this, World-Honored One? Because the World-Honored One has said that the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span...”

To have such views is not to have the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, or the view of a life-span; this is what is called the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span.
Worldly fools claim that these various views are definitively "views," but now the Buddha says they are not views, because from the very beginning they have been non-existent.
There are various views that are not real and can be corrected into the right; sentient beings are provisional, ranging from the ordinary person to the sage.
[The] correct exposition is finished. Subhūti, one who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should, regarding all phenomena...
Knowing thus, seeing thus, and resolving with faith thus, one does not give rise to the mark of dharmas.
Subhūti, what is called the "mark of dharmas" has been taught by the Tathāgata as being no mark of dharmas; it is merely designated as the "mark of dharmas."

This is not merely for immediate benefit in the present, but shall also be transmitted far into the future for a thousand ages. Since the beginning and the end have now been completed, I point to the fundamental principle to exhort people:
those who wish to resolve their minds to attain Buddhahood, purify a buddha-land, and transform sentient beings should generate knowledge and vision according to the principles explained above.
For those who possess such faith and understanding, though the principle is profound and not yet fully clear, they take faith as their basis for understanding.
The ear does not give rise to the mark of dharmas; it is merely something false and not a real dharma. The Tathāgata says that what is not a mark of dharmas is called the mark of dharmas.
When the mark is exhausted and the principle fully elucidated, it is known that only the Tathāgata speaks thus, because he declares it is not real;
therefore, one should follow it with faith.
Subhūti, if there were someone who took seven treasures filling immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds and offered them as a gift,
and if there were a son or daughter of good family who has resolved upon the bodhicitta and takes up, maintains, reads, recites,
and explains to others even as little as a four-line verse from this sutra, their merit would surpass that of the former.

The seven treasures may be exhausted, but the four lines [of this verse] are inexhaustible; it clarifies that maintaining even a single verse of this sutra with a mind of non-attainment brings merit superior to that of giving based on attainment.
How, then, should one expound it for others?
"Summoning" means to arise.
Not grasping at marks, one remains unmoving in suchness (*tathatā*).
As for the method by which this sutra is widely propagated, one must not grasp at the marks of dharmas; one must accord with the suchness of the True Suchness (*bhūtatathatā*).
Because this wisdom accords with such objects and the state of mind is harmonious, one attains the immovable and the equality of emptiness and existence. Why is this?
One should understand that all conditioned phenomena are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, shadows, dew, and lightning.

To contemplate in this manner is clear contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). One contemplates all phenomena as being like dreams, illusions, and so forth, yet for the sake of others, one speaks in verses and phrases that there are both what is real and what is conventionally existent.
This is the first of the ten similes from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: first, illusion; second, a mirage; third, the moon in water; fourth, empty space.

The five echoes, the six cities of *gandharvas*, the seven dreams, the eight shadows, the nine mirror-images, and the ten transformations—among these, six are cited from the root treatises to clarify the nine;
however, since the methods for their dissemination do not go beyond *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, they are now briefly enumerated.
Because taking *śamatha* as *vipaśyanā*, one sees that all things are empty like dreams and illusions; because taking *vipaśyanā* as *śamatha*, all dreams and illusions are [seen as such].
All are indeed suchness (*tathatā*).
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Subhūti, along with the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās,
and all the world— including devas, humans, and asuras— having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly filled with joy.
Faithfully accept and practice.
Having heard the Dharma with joy, one is able to both believe and accept it, and furthermore, act according to what has been taught.

When the speaker accords with the Dharma and the recipient receives it accordingly, they attain the true and correct Dharma of Prajñā; this is not a dharma of "attainment" such as eternalism or nihilism. These three factors must be complete.
It is sufficient to say that when a person is a disciple of the Buddha and hears the Dharma spoken by the Omniscient One— that is, the Middle Way, the True Dharma, the Prajñā of non-apprehension—
if they are a recipient of the Supreme Vehicle who has long planted the three "many" roots, and whose observance of precepts, cultivation of merit, and the three virtues are fully prepared,
they will not be startled or terrified upon hearing it, but will immediately be able to believe and understand it. Therefore, this is the Holy Path-aggregate of Rejoicing.
When the mind upholds what has been bestowed, past karmic responses are manifested; though not planned in secret, things converge spontaneously. Listening together, they awaken in unison;
the joy of the Dharma washes over the heart, and as they respectfully receive and uphold it, it shall never decay.

Regarding the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the commentaries and excerpts by various masters are beyond counting; however, the topical outline and annotations (*ke-chū*) by the Great Master Chih-i have not circulated in this land for a long time.
While Xiang-an, during his southern travels, once obtained a copy of this work and wished to publish it, the expenses required were prohibitive.
Because it is difficult to accomplish, I have been commanded to compose a verse to circulate among both the monastic and lay communities to seek generous offerings.

Should there be anyone who breaks through their stinginess, they will dissolve all states of existence within the six similes, realize Prajñā in this very moment, and ascend directly to the indestructible field of the Vajra—how joyful that would be! The verse says: [The verse follows.]
